After allele harmonization, seven of nine loci reached nominal significance (P < 0.05), and five showed directionally consistent effects with the meta-analysis ( [xref] [this file] ). 
Bulk RNA-Seq analysis identified 11,358 DEGs, comprising 4,417 upregulated and 6,941 downregulated DEGs ( [xref] [this file] ). The volcano plot illustrates the distribution of DEGs ( [xref] [rid=f3] ). 2,775 linked to immune response were retrieved from the MSigDB database ( [xref] [this file] ). The IRDGs were significantly enriched for monocyte-macrophage markers ( [xref] [this file] ), indicating their crucial role in maintaining homeostasis in the peripheral environment of AD ( [xref] [rid=f3] ). 
Integration of blood cis-eQTL data with AD GWAS summary statistics identified 45 IRDGs ( [xref] [this file] , Step 1). Subsequent integration of the same AD GWAS data with cis-mQTL summary statistics revealed 159 DNAm probes ( [xref] [this file] , Step 2). Further cross-omics integration prioritized 36 DNAm probes ( [xref] [this file] , Step 3), regulating 18 putative causal genes (SMR FDR < 0.05, HEIDI P > 0.05) through concordant cis-eQTL and cis-mQTL signals ( [xref] [rid=f4] ). Unsupervised clustering identified 19 cell types ( [xref] [this file] ). Expression profiling of six core candidate genes confirmed that PLEKHA1 was most highly expressed in NK cells among lymphocyte populations, PTK2B showed enrichment in both NK cells and CD14 Monocytes, and CD28 was predominantly expressed in Treg and CD4 TCM cells ( [xref] [this file] ), all consistent with the discovery cohort. Differential expression analysis within each cell type yielded 19 significant associations (adjusted P < 0.05): BCL3 was upregulated in CD14 Monocytes (log2FC = 0.42, P_adj = 2.18 × 10 ), CD55 was downregulated in CD4 Naive (log2FC = −0.20, P_adj = 2.41 × 10 ) and B naive cells (log2FC = −0.22, P_adj = 8.44 × 10 ¹²), CD28 was upregulated in CD8 TEM cells (log2FC = 0.088, P_adj = 1.09 × 10 ³³), and GSTK1 was consistently downregulated across CD14 Monocytes, CD8 TCM, and CD4 Naive populations ( [xref] [this file] ). Compositional analysis uncovered pronounced differences: Regulatory NK cells were almost exclusively present in AD patients (AD: 985 vs HC: 4; OR = 126.4, P_adj = 3.51 × 10 ), Early-activated NK cells were similarly enriched in AD (AD: 371 vs HC: 8; OR = 23.2, P_adj = 9.78 × 10 ³), and Activated NK cells were depleted (AD: 14.9% vs HC: 24.3%; OR = 0.55, P_adj = 2.06 × 10 ) ( [xref] [this file] ). PLEKHA1 and PTK2B were expressed across all NK subtypes ( [xref] [this file] ), though neither gene reached significant differential expression between AD and HC within individual subtypes. [xref] [this file] summarizes the mechanisms of potential drugs targeted by drug-ready genes and their possible use in AD treatment.

APOE ϵ4-stratified analyses confirmed group differences in both carrier and non-carrier subgroups ( [xref] [this file] , [xref] [this file] ). PLEKHA1 showed a nominally significant MCI versus CN difference (T = 2.11, P = 0.036, FDR P = 0.225), and TBK1 did not reach significance ( [xref] [this file] ).

Evaluation of population substructure among 36,362 individuals in the ADSP Release 4 dataset by principal component (PC) analysis identified six ancestry clusters shown in Supplementary Figure 1 [this file] : European (EA, N=16,840), African (AA, N=6,532), Caribbean Hispanic (CH, N=5,317), Native American Hispanic (NAH, N=4,722), South Asian (SA, N=2,772), and East Asian (EAS, N=178). Ancestry inference estimates highlight the genetic diversity and composition within each major ancestry group ( Supplementary Figure 2 [this file] ). After excluding individuals with missing AD status, age or sex, 26,874 individuals of diverse ancestral backgrounds remained for analysis ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
Three different PRS construction strategies were evaluated, including one based on PRS weight summation described in the Methods that was derived from the ADGC dataset ( Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). The PRS-CS weighted summation method consistently outperformed other strategies, both with and without adjustment for ɛ4 carrier status ( Supplementary Figure 3 [this file] ), and this PRS construction was employed in subsequent analyses. 
The performance of the PRS was attenuated after adjusting for ε4 and ε2 carrier status ( Supplementary Figure 4 [this file] ). PRS performance remained robust even after excluding the region, with models adjusted for ε4 and ε2 carrier status showing slightly stronger associations than unadjusted models ( Supplementary Figure 5 [this file] ). 
Further analysis showed that the association between PRS and AD risk was similar in men and women across all ancestry groups, except in the NAH group in which the PRS was not significantly associated with AD in men ( Supplementary Figure 6 [this file] ). Examination within genotype in the overall sample revealed that the association of the AD PRS was significant in all genotype groups, but the OR for ε2 carriers (1.16) was substantially smaller than the ORs for the ε3/ε3 (1.37), ε3/ε4 (1.45) and ε4/ε4 (1.52) groups ( Supplementary Figure 7 [this file] ). 
We validated the robust performance of the AD PRS in three independent cohorts: KBASE which includes 425 South Koreans ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ), AoU (version 7) which includes 71,549 individuals from diverse ancestries ( Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ), Rush comprising 897 AA participants ( Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ), and FHS which includes 4,080 EA participants ( Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). However, no sex-specific association was observed in the larger ADSP cohort ( Supplementary Figure 6 [this file] ). The AD PRS was not significant in either men or women in the Rush cohort, likely because of small sample sizes ( Supplementary Figure 8 [this file] ). 
In the ADSP dataset, our PRS showed the strongest association with AD in the AA and CH groups, but was less predictive in the NAH group compared to the score by Lourida et al . ( Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). Our PRS consistently outperformed all other scores in the Korean KBASE dataset ( Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). 
We assessed the association of AD PRS with amyloid-β 42 (Aβ42), total Tau (t-Tau), and phosphorylated Tau 181 (pTau181) measured in CSF obtained from 1,389 ADSP participants (49.7% men) whose characteristics are shown in Supplementary Table 8 [this file] . 
We also examined the association of AD PRS with plasma p-tau181 in the Framingham Heart Study (FHS; n = 1,680) and longitudinal plasma p-tau217 in the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI; n = 301) cohorts ( Supplementary Tables 8 [this file] and 9 [this file] ). A higher PRS was similarly associated with elevated p-tau217 (β = 0.20, 95% CI: 0.05−0.35, P = 8.9 × 10 ) which was evident in women (β = 0.33, 95% CI: 0.10−0.57, P = 7.6 × 10 ) but not men (β = 0.02, 95% CI: −0.17 to 0.22, P = 0.82) ( Supplementary Figure 9 [this file] ). 
We assessed the association of the AD PRS (per 1 SD increase) with AD-related neuropathological traits among ADSP participants ( Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ). A 1 SD higher AD PRS was significantly associated with greater severity across all traits: CERAD score for neuritic plaque burden (OR = 1.37, 95% CI: 1.25–1.49, = 3.95×10 ), amyloid deposition measured by Thal phase (OR = 1.38, 95% CI: 1.20–1.58, = 6.90×10 ), Braak stage (OR = 1.41, 95% CI: 1.30– 1.53, = 7.15×10 ), and AD neuropathologic change (ADNC) score (OR = 1.52, 95% CI: 1.30–1.76, = 6.80×10 ) ( Supplementary Figure 10 [this file] ). 
We assessed the association of the AD PRS with co-calibrated, harmonized and standardized scores for memory, executive function, and language, derived from longitudinal cognitive assessments across multiple time points in ADSP, KBASE, and FHS participants ( Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ). Associations of AD PRS with cognitive performance scores were significant in the EA, AA, and CH groups but not in the NAH group ( Figure 4 [rid=F4] , Supplementary Figures 11 [this file] and 12 [this file] ). Further examination of the association of the AD PRS with episodic memory and global cognition in Rush AA participants ( Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ) showed that a 1 SD higher AD PRS was significantly associated with lower episodic memory (β = −0.20, 95% CI: −0.31 to −0.10, P = 1.62 × 10 ) and global cognition (β = −0.12, 95% CI: −0.21 to −0.04, P = 5.99 × 10 ) scores ( Supplementary Figure 13 [this file] ). 
In contrast, associations of AD PRS with executive function and language scores were similar between sexes across all ancestries ( Supplementary Figures 11 [this file] and 12 [this file] ). Sex-stratified analyses in the Rush and KBASE cohorts yielded comparable results ( Supplementary Figure 13 [this file] ). 
Further analysis of cognitive trajectories by sex and revealed no significant differences in the slope or level of decline across PRS strata between males and females in the overall sample ( Supplementary Figure 14 [this file] ). 
We examined the association of AD PRS with hippocampal volume using longitudinal FreeSurfer-derived structural MRI data from ADSP (n= 6,568) and FHS (n= 970) participants ages 60 and older ( Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ). This association was observed separately in both women and men in ADSP (women: β = −0.024, 95% CI: −0.035 to −0.014, P = 3.14 × 10 ; men: β = −0.016, 95% CI: −0.028 to −0.005, P = 6.60 × 10 ), whereas in FHS the association was evident only in women (β = −0.019, 95% CI: −0.035 to −0.003, P = 2.33 × 10 ) and not men (β = −0.017, 95% CI: −0.036 to 0.002, P = 0.073) ( Supplementary Figure 15 [this file] ). 
For this analysis, we identified and removed overlapping individuals between the ADGC and the ADSP datasets, as detailed in Supplementary Note 1 [this file] . Further details of the genotyping and quality controls are provided in Supplementary Note 1 [this file] .

Additional details on WGS and quality control procedures are provided in Supplementary Note 5 [this file] . 
Population ancestry was determined from clusters derived by PCA as described in Supplementary Note 6 [this file] . Details for assessing relatedness and population substructure using the GENESIS R package are provided in Supplementary Note 7 [this file] . 
Summation weights were derived from the ADGC dataset, and the mean and SD of the final PRS calculated in the ADSP cohort are reported in Supplementary Table 13 [this file] . 
Study accession numbers and corresponding publications are provided in Supplementary Tables 6 [this file] and 7 [this file] . 
We examined the association between AD PRS and AD-related phenotypes using data from multiple cohorts listed in Supplementary Table 14 [this file] .

CN-LOH showed the strongest association (OR = 1.40, 95% CI = 1.21−1.63, = 8.8 × 10 ; Fig. 1b [rid=F1] and Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ), with nominally significant association in all separated ancestries ( < 0.05). 
The mCA-associated risk tested in all ancestries combined appeared to be stronger among ε4 non-carriers (OR = 1.16 vs 1.31 for the presence of any mCA types between APOE4 carriers and non-carriers in all ancestries; Fig. 1c [rid=F1] and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). However, when stratified by ancestry, the tendency varied, with stronger associations observed among ε4 non-carriers in Europeans (EUR) (OR = 1.00 vs 1.32, = 0.033), whereas in South Asians (SAS), stronger associations were seen among ε4 carriers (OR = 6.73 vs 1.16, = 0.021; Supplementary Fig. 2 [rid=SD1] and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). Our results suggested regional heterogeneity, with the gain on chromosomes 1 and 8 showing the most significant association (OR = 5.88, 95% CI = 1.68−20.53, = 0.0055 for chromosome 1 and OR = 2.45, 95% CI = 1.40−4.42, = 0.0052 for chromosome 8; Fig. 1e [rid=F1] and Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
In our data, CHIP was significantly associated with an increased AD risk (OR = 1.30, 95% CI = 1.16−1.46, = 4.2 × 10 ; Fig. 1g [rid=F1] and Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). When both mCAs and CHIP were included in the same model, each remained independently associated with AD ( = 5.1 × 10 and 1.1 × 10 , respectively; Supplementary Fig. 3 [rid=SD1] and Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ), with no significant interaction effect detected ( = 0.88).

An in-depth overview of all methodologies is provided in the eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
Case-control, family-based, and longitudinal AD genetic cohorts from the Alzheimer’s Disease Genetics Consortium (ADGC) and Alzheimer’s Disease Sequencing Project (ADSP) (release 3) were available through public repositories with genetic data from SNV microarrays and whole-genome sequencing (eTable 1 and 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). These cohorts contributed clinically diagnosed AD cases and have similar sample demographic characteristics (40.0% pathology verified; eTable 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
ADGC and ADSP data underwent extensive quality control and imputation to the Trans-Omics for Precision Medicine reference panel (eTable 4 and 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Specific consideration was given to X chromosome quality control, as in prior work (eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Non-Hispanic White, European ancestry individuals with AD and control individuals, carrying XX or XY with concordant self-reported sex and ages older than 60 years (older than 18 years and a median of 63 years in FinnGen), were retained for analyses (eFigure 1, eTable 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Variants were filtered using cohort-specific minor allele frequency criteria, which on average correspond to a minor allele frequency greater than 0.05% (eTable 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
To maximize power, the health registry and proxy status were unified into a single phenotype, following a model for random XCI, for which association coefficients were adjusted onto a regular case-control scale (eTables 6 and 7 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). After rescaling, UKB showed consistent coefficient distributions with ADGC and ADSP (eFigure 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
We leveraged public datasets where quantitative trait loci for expression and protein levels were available for the X chromosome in brain and nonbrain tissues (eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
A total of 1 152 284 individuals (664 403 [57.7%] female and 487 881 [42.3%] male; 138 558 with AD [15 081 clinically diagnosed and 41 091 health registry confirmed] and 82 386 proxy individuals) were included in the XWAS (eTable 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] ), with an estimated effective sample size of 487 588. There was no sign of genomic inflation (eFigure 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Using all data, we associated 2 rare (minor allele frequency less than 1%) lead variants in the and loci and 4 common lead variants in the , , , and loci ( Figure 1 [rid=noi240054f1] B, Table 1 [rid=noi240054t1] ; locus zoom and forest plots in eFigures 4 and 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). All common variant loci showed colocalization for at least 1 nearby gene in brain tissue ( Table 2 [rid=noi240054t2] ; eTable 8 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). The overall top association signal (cross-cohort allele frequencies in eTable 9 in Supplement 1 [this file] ), intronic on , passed conservative significance criteria (OR, 1.03; 95% CI, 1.02-1.04) and showed colocalization for several genes, most notably and . Colocalization plots for top prioritized genes are in eFigures 6-10 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
Evaluation of evidence for escape from XCI and sex-specific effect sizes are provided in Figure 3 and eTable 10 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
When evaluating lead variants from the nonstratified analyses for evidence of escape from XCI with regard to AD risk ( Figure 3 [rid=noi240054f3] ; eTable 10 in Supplement 1 [this file] ), escape was not apparent for the and lead variants but was apparent for , , , and . The lead variant furthermore displayed a significant female-biased heterogeneity effect (eTable 10 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Additional evaluation of XCI escape, including subthreshold signals from male- and female-stratified XWASs, further supported apparent escape from XCI for some common, small effect size variants (eFigure 11 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
All nonstratified lead variants for the 6 independent risk loci are shown reporting their sex-specific odds ratios (ORs), as well as the ratio of male to female β coefficients to assess evidence for escape from XCI (eTable 10 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Although no colocalization support was observed for at this locus, it may still be linked to the AD association signal through other mechanisms that we could not explore here. and are highly conserved genes that regulate pH homeostasis in Golgi secretory compartments and endosomes and might thus be expected to contribute to increased amyloid accumulation across aging when their expression levels are increased (a potential mechanistic hypothesis is provided in the eDiscussion in Supplement 1 [this file] ). In line with this expectation, quantitative trait loci data support that the top risk allele in the locus was associated with increased expression of in brain tissue, increasing expression by 8% to 22% under an XCI model (eTable 11 in Supplement 1 [this file] ).

In comparison, the TOPMed-r2 panel included 295 million variants (274,388,520 [92.85%] SNVs and 20,899,436 [7.15%] indels in chromosomes 1–22) derived from 97,256 sequenced genomes, 48.49% European, 24.95% African, 17.57% admixed American, 1.22% East Asian, 0.66% South Asian, and 7.11% unassigned-ethnic individuals ( Table S1 [this file] ). 
With this larger sample set, 65.38% (68 out of 104) SVs exhibited an increase in allele count, and 39.71% (27 out of 68) showed enhanced statistical significance ( Table S2 [this file] ). 
Of note, 10 out of 55 indels were absent in TOPMed-r2 imputation ( Table S3 [this file] ), which are in genes, C12orf81, TOMM20L, FAM174B, NTN3, RGL3, PNKP, PPDPF, and PCDHB13. 
To evaluate the accuracy of imputed genotypes for those disease susceptibility indels, PCR validation was conducted on six indels, which are located in DNAH14, ANO7, ZNF655, PTGER1, SCRT2, and PPDPF, on 17 available DNA samples from the ADGC cohorts ( Table S4 [this file] ). 
For those well-imputed SNVs and indels, 75.38% (49 out of 65) showed an increase in allele counts as sample size expanded, and 67.35% (33 out of 49) increased statistical significance ( Table S5 [this file] ). 
The ADSP-Short-Var panel demonstrated improved performance over the TOPMed-r2 panel for variants with MAF < 0.0005 in Hispanic cohorts and performed comparably well for variants with MAF < 0.0005 in NHW cohorts ( Figure 2 [rid=F2] , Table S6 [this file] ). 
Both false positive (FP) and true positive (TP) SVs decreased as the R threshold increased ( Table S7 [this file] ). 
Our analysis on pooled samples across ethnicities revealed eight genome-wide significant loci, including 495 genome-wide significant variants across 36 genes, that were concordant in all three association tests ( Table S8 [this file] ). 
Ethnicity-specific analysis in NHW cohorts (Ncase=13,182 and Ncontrol=15,216) revealed eight genome-wide significant loci, including 765 genome-wide significant variants across 44 genes, in all three association tests ( Table S8 [this file] ). Two loci on chromosomes 1 and 3 emerged, suggesting that the approach for pooled samples might obscure specific genetic signals due to differences in population genetic structures ( Table S9 [this file] ). 
Upon comparing the results of single variant association tests on pooled samples (Ncase=16,779 and Ncontrol=21,492) imputations from the ADSP-Short-Var and ADSP-All-Var panels, we identified eight consensus genome-wide significant loci across 36 genes ( Table S8 [this file] ) in both tests ( Figure 5 [rid=F5] ). 
These changes may result in differing outcomes when the same covariates are adjusted in association tests between imputations from the two panels, despite the AFs being quite similar ( Table S10 [this file] ).

The number of variants unique to each test was 7 for ADSP-Short-Var, 21 for TOPMed-r2, and 14 for meta-imputation ( Figures S8B [this file] and S9C [this file] ).

This stringent filtering resulted in a final dataset of 16,564 sequenced genomes with 51,459,037 SNVs and 3,322,380 indels for a reference panel construction ( Figure S12A [this file] ).

Notably, genotype calls for deletions exhibited superior quality with a lower missing genotype rate compared to duplications, insertions, and inversions ( Fig. S1 [this file] ). 
However, the third principal component of SVs is associated with read length and sequencing platforms ( Fig. S2 [this file] ), indicating batch effect is an important confounding factor to consider when performing SV analysis. 
Among 400,234 SVs, 94,923 (24%) are singletons, and 232,295 (58%) are rare with AF < 1% ( Fig. S3 [this file] ). 
Evaluation of the sensitivity of SV calling pipeline using synthetic mutations ( Methods [rid=S10] ) revealed a sensitivity of 99.4% for 4,000 deletions and 94.4% for 1,500 inversions ( Table S2 [this file] ). 
Approximately 50% of the high-quality SVs were detected in the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD, 292,307 SV sites), but there was less overlap with SVs in the 1000 Genomes Project (1KG, 66,505 SV sites) ( Fig. S4 [this file] ). The SV callset before high-quality filtering had a higher recall (a higher percentage of SVs from gnomAD and 1KG) at the cost of lower precision (a lower percentage of SVs confirmed by gnomAD and 1KG) ( Fig. S4 [this file] , Fig. S5 [this file] ). 
Of 95 SVs selected for experimental validation ( Table S3 [this file] ; Methods [rid=S10] ), 78 were confirmed, resulting in a sensitivity rate of 82%. On individual genotype level, an accuracy of 89% was achieved for 276 called genotypes for 95 SVs undergoing PCR validation ( Table S4 [this file] ), and this value increased to 92% for 207 called genotypes for 72 high-quality SVs ( Table S4 [this file] ). 
Ten rare SVs ( Table S5 [this file] ) were replicated in our SV callset. A 417 Kb duplication ( Fig. S6 [this file] ) covering the is identified in one individual with early onset of AD at his age of 52. Tau PET uptake showed an early slight increase in early Braak stage regions, with progressive increases in later regions from pseudotime ~0.50 (when eMTBR-tau243 also accelerated) (details in appendix p2 [this file] and appendix p8 [this file] ). 
In Knight ADRC (N=80, appendix p4 [this file] ), we observed increased %p-tau217 already in people with still sparse Aβ plaque pathology (CERAD Sparse vs. None, P=0.035) and tau tangle pathology restricted mainly to the temporal lobe (Braak stage IV, vs. stages I [P=0.00033], II [P=0.00053] and III [P=0.013]), while eMTBR-tau243 was increased only with frequent plaque pathology (CERAD Frequent vs. None, P<0.0001) and widespread neocortical tau tangle pathology (Braak stage V, vs. stage I, P=0.045) ( Figure 1B [rid=F1] – E [rid=F1] ). 
Post-hoc, we restricted analyses to %p-tau217 positive SCD patients, where eMTBR-tau243 positives had more steep decline in all cognitive tests over time (and greater tau burden at baseline) compared to eMTBR-tau243 negative SCD ( appendix p9 [this file] – 10 [this file] ). 
When excluding the SCD patients, PPV was still markedly improved when combining eMTBR-tau243 and %p-tau217, but the NPV was lower than in the main analysis (66% instead of 77%) ( appendix p11 [this file] ) 
Testing of eMTBR-tau243 in other diagnostic groups showed no links between eMTBR-tau243 and non-AD dementias ( appendix p2 [this file] ). 
We repeated the main analyses in 52 cognitively impaired participants in the Knight ADRC cohort (39 CDR 0.5, 12 CDR 1, and one CDR 2; appendix p6 [this file] ), using the same definitions as in the main analyses. 52% (N=27) had established AD and 83% (N=43) were positive for %p-tau217. 
We consider these %p-tau217 and eMTBR-tau243 positive SCDs likely to be “at risk” for AD, following the IWG terminology, especially since they had increased tau PET burden and accelerated longitudinal cognitive decline, compared to eMTBR-tau243 negative SCD ( appendix p9 [this file] – 10 [this file] ).

While our primary analyses found no association between average brain connectivity and tau laterality, we further investigated whether connectivity relates to overall tau burden (see Supplementary S2 [this file] ). Compared to A-T- cognitively unimpaired controls, A+T+ individuals exhibited significantly lower average connectivity across the whole brain (functional: β = −0.184, p = 0.028; structural: β = −0.387, p < 0.001) including inter-hemispheric connections (functional: β = −0.186, p = 0.027; structural: β = −0.190, p = 0.012) after adjusting for age and sex (Fig. S2.4 [this file] ). Edge-wise, within A+T+ individuals, lower functional and structural connectivity between homotopic regions was associated with higher bilateral tau burden in multiple regions across the brain, with the strongest effects observed in occipital and temporal areas for functional connectivity and across the neocortex except the temporal lobe for structural connectivity (Fig. S2.2 [this file] ). Second, to address potential confounding effects of regional variability in tau load, three additional composite ROIs were defined based on the ranking of group-average tau SUVR values from A+T+ subjects (i.e., high tau burden corresponds to regions above the 75 percentile, medium tau burden corresponds to regions between the 25 and the 75 percentile and low tau burden corresponds to regions below the 25 percentile; see Supplementary S2 [this file] ). After adjusting for age, sex, and bilateral tau load, neither average inter-hemispheric (Fig. S2.5 [this file] ; functional: all p > 0.8; structural: all p > 0.2) nor intra-hemispheric connectivity (Fig. S2.6 [this file] ; functional: all p > 0.4; structural: all p > 0.5) showed significant associations with absolute tau laterality in any of these composite ROIs. 
Additional analyses based on a priori selected meta-ROIs revealed the strongest associations between global Aβ laterality and tau laterality were present in a meta-ROI encompassing regions included in Braak stages III-IV (Fig. S2.7 [this file] ; β = 0.655, 95%CI = [0.556; 0.754], p < 0.001). In particular, temporal regions showed the strongest average association with all brain regions (inferior temporal: β = 0.428; fusiform: β = 0.405; middle temporal: β = 0.405; see Fig. S2.8 [this file] in Supplementary S2 [this file] ). 
To confirm the association between the laterality of Aβ and tau, we performed the same analyses on three independent cohorts – Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) , Anti-Amyloid Treatment in Asymptomatic Alzheimer’s Disease (A4) , and Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) – out of which only A+T+ subjects were included (see Supplementary Table S2.9 [this file] for demographics). Interestingly, all replication cohorts showed the greatest effect size of spatial relationship between the laterality of tau and Aβ pathologies in regions within Braak stages III and IV (see Fig. S2.9 [this file] in Supplementary 2 [this file] ). 
To support that the results did not arise from methodological issues, we performed a set of sensitivity analyses in the main cohort (see Supplementary S2 [this file] for a detailed overview). First, we investigated the association between the two pathologies using PET SUVR values corrected for partial volume effects (see Fig. S2.10 [this file] ) and found consistent results across the brain (global: β = 0.648, p < 0.001) and within all meta-ROIs defined based on Braak stages (I-II: β = 0.178, p = 0.016; III-IV: β = 0.728, p < 0.001; V-VI: β = 0.590, p < 0.001). Second, the association between the laterality of tau and Aβ remained essentially the same when adjusting for laterality of cerebral blood flow measured with arterial spin labelling (ASL; global: β = 0.498, p < 0.001) or cortical thickness (global: β = 0.560, p < 0.001) in the model (see Fig. S2.12 [this file] ). SILA models individual Aβ accumulation curves to estimate the timing of hemispheric Aβ onset (see Supplementary S2 [this file] ). Asymmetric tau groups exhibited significantly larger inter-hemispheric differences in estimated global Aβ onset (left asymmetric: Δ = 1.7 years, p = 0.006; right asymmetric: Δ = 2.5 years, p < 0.001) compared to the symmetric group (Δ = 1.3 years; Fig. S2.13 [this file] ), suggesting earlier regional Aβ accumulation may contribute to tau lateralisation. Finally, Aβ-PET and tau-PET scans for nine representative cases (i.e., three cases for each asymmetrical profile) can be seen in Supplementary S3 [this file] . 
We then further stratified the sample based on baseline temporal meta-ROI tau-PET uptake to A+T- (n = 180) and A+T+ (n = 109) groups (see Table S2.2 [this file] for demographics) and repeated the analyses according to regions defined in Braak stages. For an overview of the models, see Supplementary Table S2 [this file] .3, S2 [this file] .4, and S2.5 [this file] . 
For an overview of the models, see Supplementary Table S2 [this file] .6 and S2.7 [this file] . 
To further confirm that these findings were not a result of our methodological choices, we repeated the analysis using partial volume corrected PET SUVR values (see Supplementary S2 [this file] ). Most of the findings were successfully replicated with most notably the full A+ sample exhibiting even stronger effect (see Fig. S2.11 [this file] ; β = 0.041, 95%CI = [0.021; 0.060], p < 0.001) than our main analysis, but there were also some exceptions. Higher baseline absolute tau laterality was associated with a steeper increase in tau load in Braak III-IV (β = 0.085, p < 0.001) and V-VI (β = 0.114, p < 0.001) regions, while baseline Aβ laterality showed no effect (see Fig. S2.14 [this file] ). Neither functional nor structural connectivity improved model fits (all p > 0.6) or reached significance as predictors, indicating negligible explanatory power beyond Aβ asymmetry (see Supplementary S2 [this file] ). 
Direction of tau lateralisation (left vs right asymmetry) did not influence cognitive trajectories (see Fig. S2.15 [this file] in Supplementary S2 [this file] ). See Supplementary Table S2.8 [this file] for an overview of the models. 
Both clinically unimpaired and impaired individuals were included if they met the previously mentioned criteria (see Supplementary S1 [this file] for detailed inclusion and exclusion criteria). Aβ positivity was defined using a previously established cut-off (SUVR > 1.033) determined via Gaussian mixture modelling (GMM) applied on the Aβ-PET uptake in a neocortical composite meta-ROI (regions detailed in Table S1.1 [this file] ), based on data from both the cognitively unimpaired and impaired individuals in the BioFINDER-2 cohort . 
The cross-sectional subsample of 475 participants included only A+ individuals who were also tau positive (T+) as defined by tau-PET uptake in a temporal meta-ROI (i.e., Braak stages I-IV regions; detailed in Table S1.1 [this file] ). 
This subsample was stratified into A+T- (n = 180) and A+T+ (n = 109) based on the tau positivity at baseline (see Supplementary Table S2.2 [this file] for demographics). 
The average SUVR values were also calculated for meta-ROIs: global (i.e., whole brain), temporal (i.e., Braak I-IV), Braak I-II, Braak III-IV, Braak V-VI, Early-Aβ, Intermediate-Aβ, and Late-Aβ (Fig. 8 [rid=Fig8] ; see Supplementary Table S1.1 [this file] for detailed overview) . 
See Supplementary S1 [this file] for a more detailed description of the process. 
To reduce noise and focus on the most biologically plausible connections, we masked both the FC and SC matrices for all subjects by selecting only the top 10% inter-hemispheric connections identified in 294 age-matched healthy controls with no evidence of Aβ or tau pathology from the BioFINDER-2 cohort (see Supplementary S1 [this file] for more information). 
The primary NBS analyses were performed on the masked matrices (retaining the top 10% strongest connections from healthy controls; see Supplementary S1 [this file] for more information on masking) to focus on biologically plausible connections. 
Three external cohorts (see Table S2.9 [this file] for demographics) were used to validate the association between the laterality of Aβ and tau distribution – Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3; https://sites.wustl.edu/oasisbrains/ (https://sites.wustl.edu/oasisbrains/) ), Anti-Amyloid Treatment in Asymptomatic Alzheimer’s Disease (A4; https://www.a4studydata.org/ (https://www.a4studydata.org/) ), and Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI; https://adni.loni.usc.edu/ (https://adni.loni.usc.edu/) ).

Aβ42/40 by itself (0.849; 95% CI, 0.810-0.887; <.001)
(eFigure 1 and eTable 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] ).

addition, we did not find any improvement in AUCs when adding plasma p-tau231 or GFAP to

in Supplement

[8.3] years) from the Knight ADRC cohort (eTable 10 in Supplement 1 [this file] ), of

(0.855; 95% CI, 0.810-0.900; <.001) (eFigure 1 and eTable 11 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Similar to the BioFINDER-2 study, discriminative accuracies for Aβ-PET status at

In participants with missing CSF data, Aβ-positivity was determined from EDTA plasma Aβ /Aβ ratios ( Supplementary material [this file] , Methods section). 
ASHS was implemented using an in-house longitudinal segmentation pipeline if usable follow-up structural MRI data were available ( Supplementary material [this file] , Methods section). Average cortical thickness was calculated for temporal, parietal, frontal and occipital regions of interest based on FreeSurfer’s Desikan–Killiany parcellation ( Supplementary material [this file] , Methods section). 
Further details on SuStaIn modelling parameters, internal 10-fold cross-validation, model selection, longitudinal model validation and subsample replication are provided in the Supplementary material [this file] , Methods section. 
To ensure comparability with DELCODE, only BioFINDER-2 participants aged ≥60 years and who belonged to the CU ( = 283), SCD ( = 152), MCI ( = 212) or DAT ( = 132) diagnostic groups were included (see Palmqvist . and Supplementary material [this file] , Methods for inclusion criteria). 
Further methodological details for the BioFINDER-2 sample are provided in the Supplementary material [this file] , Methods section. 
In the remaining 354 participants, two distinct atrophy progression sequences were identified ( Fig. 1A and C [rid=awae118-F1] , Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] and Supplementary material [this file] , Results section). 
Analyses of follow-up MRI scans revealed that most observed atrophy trajectories (92.52% of participants with limbic-predominant and 86.24% of participants with baseline hippocampal-sparing atrophy) were in line with the modelled atrophy sequences ( Supplementary material [this file] , Results section). Evidence for highly similar atrophy subtypes was found in the Aβ-positive and CU/SCD subsamples ( Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] and Supplementary material [this file] , Results section). 
Baseline characteristics of individuals in both atrophy subtypes were compared with the atrophy-negative group ( Fig. 2A–E [rid=awae118-F2] and Supplementary Tables 1 and 2 [this file] ). 
Next, the two subtypes were contrasted against each other with the hippocampal-sparing subtype as the reference group ( Fig. 2C and F [rid=awae118-F2] and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). Raw data are depicted in Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] . 
In only Aβ-positive participants, there was no significant association of atrophy subtype with demographics and fluid AD biomarkers, while the relationships of atrophy subtype with cognitive scores were replicated ( Supplementary Tables 4–6 [this file] ). 
In both subtypes, PACC-5 slopes were negatively related to SuStaIn stage, with stronger interaction effects of Time × SuStaIn stage in the limbic-predominant subtype ( = −0.05, = 0.15, = 0.002) than in the hippocampal-sparing subtype ( = −0.03, = 0.08, = 0.005; Fig. 3F and G [rid=awae118-F3] and Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). 
A similar trend was observed in the limbic-predominant subtype ( = −0.07, = 0.07, = 0.077; Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). 
Decline on the PACC-5 was steeper with increasing SuStaIn stage in the hippocampal-sparing ( = −0.03, = 0.07, = 0.019) but not the limbic-predominant ( = −0.01, = 0.01, = 0.580) atrophy subtype ( Fig. 3I and J [rid=awae118-F3] and Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). 
Receiver operating characteristic curves for all models are shown in Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] . Model summaries are provided in Supplementary Table 10 [this file] . 
SuStaIn modelling naïve to the main DELCODE model successfully replicated the two atrophy progression sequences in the BioFINDER-2 sample ( Fig. 5A [rid=awae118-F5] and Supplementary material [this file] , Results section). 
There was no difference in mPACC scores between atrophy subtypes ( Supplementary Table 11 [this file] and Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). 
In both subtypes, increasing SuStaIn stages were linked to faster-declining mPACC scores ( Supplementary Table 12 [this file] and Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ).

Demographic information is presented in Table 1 [rid=Tab1] (see Supplementary Table 1 [this file] for demographic information by diagnostic groups). More detailed information about vascular risk factors and pathologies is provided in Supplementary Table 1 [this file] , and a description of the diagnosis for non-AD patients can be found in Supplementary Table 2 [this file] . Of these, 220 participants had longitudinal CSF data available (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
CSF biomarker levels by stage can be found in Fig. 1b [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Table 4 [this file] . We found that none of the vascular risks (hypertension, hyperlipidemia or diabetes) nor vascular pathologies (white matter lesions, lacunes, ischemic infarcts, hemorrhages, microbleeds or siderosis) have an effect on our model (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] and Supplementary Figs. 1 [this file] and 2 [this file] ). 
Finally, we assessed the stability of our model using the longitudinal CSF data over a mean (s.d.) of 2.1 (0.2) years ( = 220; Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). Of note, participants with longitudinal CSF information had lower levels of pathology as measured by main biomarkers than those without longitudinal CSF data, even while having similar demographic characteristics (Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
Statistics of each of these AD biomarkers and their differences per CSF stage can be found in Supplementary Table 6 [this file] . 
For tau-PET, we quantified the signal in different brain regions, using the previously validated regions of interest (ROIs) reflecting the different Braak stages (Extended Data Fig. 4 [rid=Fig11] and Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). We also examined different measures of cognitive function, including composites for memory, executive, language and visuospatial functions, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 5 [rid=Fig12] and Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). 
Using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses, we determined that CSF stage 2 was the optimal threshold for predicting amyloid-PET positivity with high accuracy (area under the curve and 95% confidence interval (AUC (95% CI) = 0.96 (0.93, 0.98), sensitivity = 0.93 and specificity = 0.89, first column; Fig. 3b [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 9 [this file] )). Tau-PET positivity was also predicted with high accuracy when using CSF stage 4 as a threshold (AUC (95% CI) = 0.95 (0.93, 0.97), sensitivity = 0.91 and specificity = 0.92, second column; Fig. 3b [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). 
We observed that higher CSF stages were associated with higher predicted probabilities of being at more advanced A/T PET status (c-index (95% CI) = 0.95 (0.93, 0.97), last column; Fig. 3b [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). Similarly, higher CSF stages were associated with more advanced PET-based stages although with slightly lower accuracy (c-index (95% CI) = 0.92 (0.90, 0.94); Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). 
Higher CSF stages were associated with more advanced cognitive stages (c-index (95% CI) = 0.88 (0.86, 0.91), first column; Fig. 3c [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). Here, we also had a good predictive accuracy (c-index (95% CI) = 0.87 (0.84,0.89)), and we observed the expected pattern, with participants with subjective cognitive decline (SCD) mainly included in CSF stages 1–3 (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). Participants at CSF stage 2 or higher with objective cognitive impairment had a high probability of having AD as the cause of their cognitive impairment (AUC (95% CI) = 0.95 (0.93, 0.98), sensitivity = 0.97 and specificity = 0.75, last column; Fig. 3c,d [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
Next, we used longitudinal imaging and cognitive data to assess how AD biomarkers change over time based on the baseline CSF stage classification (Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ). The rate of accumulation of Aβ aggregates as measured with PET ( = 218) increased at early CSF stages, reaching the highest values at CSF stage 2, and, thereafter, the rate decreased but still remained positive (Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ). 
When adjusting for age, sex and clinical status at baseline (that is, CU or MCI), the hazard ratio (HR) was 5.2 (95% CI: 2.2, 12.6, < 0.001), when comparing participants at CSF stages 4 or 5 to participants at lower, but positive, CSF stages (1–3; Fig. 5b [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ). When including only those with MCI at baseline (progressors: 38/88), we still found that those at CSF stages 4 or 5 at baseline had a significantly higher probability to progress to AD dementia (HR (95% CI) = 4.5 (1.8, 10.8), < 0.001; Fig. 5c,d [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ). Again, those CU participants at higher CSF stages (4–5) at baseline were much more prone to progress to MCI with an HR of 16.0 (95% CI: 3.2, 81.1, < 0.001; Fig. 5e,f [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ) compared to those in stage 1–3, and 50% already progressed to MCI after 4.1 years, supporting the clinical utility of the proposed staging model. 
Nonetheless, the overall behavior of these CSF biomarkers by the biomarker stages was similar to that in the main cohort (Fig. 6b [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). Furthermore, the other AD biomarkers available (not included in the CSF staging model) showed similar trajectories to those in the main sample (Fig. 6c [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). Details of participant characteristics (Extended Data Fig. 2 [rid=Fig9] ), tau-PET binding in different regions (Extended Data Fig. 4 [rid=Fig11] and Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ) and other cognitive measures (Extended Data Fig. 5 [rid=Fig12] and Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ) per CSF stage can be found in the Extended Data. Stability analyses, within participants with available longitudinal CSF measures ( = 51; Supplementary Table 13 [this file] ), also showed that most participants remained at the same stage ( = 46, 90.2%) or progressed ( = 4, 7.8%) at follow-up (Extended Data Fig. 3c,d [rid=Fig10] ). 
As in the case of BioFINDER-2, CSF stage 2 was optimal for predicting amyloid-PET positivity (AUC (95% CI) = 0.89 (0.85, 0.94); Fig. 6d,g [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ), whereas CSF stage 4 was optimal for predicting tau-PET positivity (AUC (95% CI) = 0.94 (0.91, 0.96); Fig. 6e,h [rid=Fig6] ). Consistent with findings in BioFINDER-2, higher CSF stages were predictive of more advanced A/T stages, as assessed by PET (c-index (95% CI) = 0.89 (0.86, 0.92); Fig. 6f,i [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). 
We found that CU (CDR = 0) and very mild AD (CDR = 0.5) participants at the highest CSF stages (4–5) exhibited an increased risk (HR (95% CI) = 6.9 (3.0, 16.0), < 0.001) of progressing to AD dementia (CDR ≥ 1) at follow-up, even when adjusting for age, sex and clinical status (that is, CDR = 0 or CDR = 0.5) at baseline, compared to participants at CSF stages 1–3 (Fig. 6j,k [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ). Similarly, CU participants at higher CSF stages (that is, 4–5) had higher risk (HR (95% CI) = 4.2 (2.0, 8.8), < 0.001) of progressing to very mild AD or more advanced disease stages when compared to participants at lower, but positive, CSF stages (1–3; Fig. 6l,m [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ), with 50% of them progressing after 3.0 years, whereas, for the 1–3 group, it took 7.6 years. 
We included only one non-phosphorylated peptide due to the extremely high correlation that all have among them ( ≥ 0.98; Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). 
We observed that the high correlation between the different np-tau variants prevented the algorithm from finding a clear ordering among them but not for the other included AD biomarkers (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). Next, we created new models using different np-tau fragments that rendered very similar results ( Supplementary Methods [this file] ). Finally, we simulated new datasets with two and three underlying subtypes to assess the minimal size a subtype must be to be detected by SuStaIn ( Supplementary Methods [this file] ). We observed that SuStaIn was able to detect two and three underlying subtypes until the smaller subtypes included more than 5% of the original sample (Supplementary Figs. 8 [this file] and 9 [this file] ). 
We first started with seven biomarkers and tested the optimal number of subtypes, which was, again, one (CVIC: subtype 1 = 629.5, subtype 2 = 649.4, subtype 3 = 658.4, log-likelihood: subtype 1 = −32.3, subtype 2 = −33.3, subtype 3 = −33.8; Supplementary Fig. 10a [this file] ). Based on CVIC (model 1: 629.5, model 2: 590.1, model 3: 564.6, model 4: 567.1, model 5: 520.7, model 6: 524.0 and model 7: 497.2) and log-likelihood (median: model 1: −31.8, model 2: −29.8, model 3: −28.1, model 4: −28.4, model 5: −25.9, model 6: −26.1 and model 7: −24.8) metrics, the model with only pT217/T217 (model 7) was again selected as the optimal (Supplementary Fig. 10b [this file] ). Finally, we created models for 1–3 subtypes and based on CVIC (subtypes: 1 = 497.2, 2 = 524.5 and 3 = 550.6) and log-likelihood (median: 1 = −24.8, 2 = −27.0 and 3 = −28.3), and the less complex model (that is, one subtype) was selected as the best fit to the data (Supplementary Fig. 10c [this file] ).

Similar results were obtained when using clinical visual reads to determine Aβ PET status (Extended Data Fig. 1a [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). Similar results were also found in the Knight ADRC cohort, where plasma %p-tau217 had an overall accuracy of 94% (95% CI: 72%, 100%), a PPV of 99% (95% CI: 97%, 100%) and an NPV of 89% (95% CI: 48%, 100%), which was clinically equivalent to the performances of FDA-approved CSF Lumipulse Aβ42/40 (accuracy, 78% (95% CI: 44%, 98%); PPV, 98% (95% CI: 96%, 100%); NPV, 62% (95% CI: 32%, 100%)) and CSF Lumipulse p-tau181/Aβ42 (accuracy, 91% (95% CI: 68%, 100%); PPV, 99% (95% CI: 97%, 100%); NPV, 82% (95% CI: 45%, 100%)) (Supplementary Fig. 1a [this file] and Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
In the Knight ADRC cohort, the diagnostic metrics of plasma %p-tau217 were clinically equivalent to those of the CSF measures (Supplementary Fig. 2a,c [this file] and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
Similar results were obtained when FDA-approved visual reads were used to determine the Aβ PET status (Extended Data Fig. 1b [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ) and in the Knight ADRC cohort (Supplementary Fig. 1b [this file] and Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
The results obtained in Knight ADRC showed a similar performance between plasma and CSF biomarkers (Supplementary Fig. 2b [this file] and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
A description of specific diagnosis for the cognitively impaired participants is shown in Supplementary Table 4 [this file] . In cognitively impaired individuals in the BioFINDER-2 cohort, we found that blood plasma %p-tau217 exhibited an AUC of 0.94 (95% CI: 0.92, 0.96) in distinguishing individuals with and without symptomatic AD (Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ), which was clinically equivalent to CSF p-tau181/Aβ42 (95%, 95% CI: 93%, 96%) and CSF Aβ42/40 (93%, 95% CI: 91%, 95%). Furthermore, plasma %p-tau217 had an overall accuracy of 86% (95% CI: 82%, 89%), a PPV of 89% (95% CI: 87%, 91%) and an NPV of 84% (95% CI: 77%, 89%) (Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). Applying the two-cutoffs approach increased the diagnostic metrics to 93–94%, with 24% of the participants in the intermediate group (Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
These results were in line with the previous analyses, showing that plasma %p-tau217 was clinically equivalent to CSF biomarkers for predicting Aβ PET positivity using a single-cutoff approach (Supplementary Fig. 3a [this file] and Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ) and a two-cutoffs approach (Supplementary Fig. 3b [this file] and Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). For tau PET, we generally observed higher estimates of plasma %p-tau217 compared to the two CSF biomarkers (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] and Supplementary Tables 7 [this file] and 8 [this file] ). 
Plasma %p-tau217 cutoffs were derived in Knight ADRC participants and CSF biomarker cutoffs in participants from the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) ( Supplementary Methods [this file] ). In brief, the performances of plasma %p-tau217 were clinically equivalent to or slightly higher than those of CSF biomarkers when using both the single-cutoff approach (Extended Data Fig. 3a [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ) and the two-cutoffs approach (Extended Data Fig. 3b [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ) for prediction of Aβ positivity. 
In summary, the differences between these two approaches were very small, as can be observed in Supplementary Figs. 5 [this file] and 6 [this file] and in Supplementary Tables 9 [this file] and 10 [this file] . 
Only one (2.5%) of these participants changed %ptau217 biomarker status during follow-up testing, supporting the consistency of plasma %p-tau217 measures when plasma sampling and %ptau217 testing is repeated (Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ). 
Blood plasma p-tau217 and non-p-tau217 were measured by liquid chromatography–tandem high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC–MS/HRMS) analysis as detailed in the Supplementary Methods [this file] . 
Second, we also derived the plasma %p-tau217 cutoffs in the Knight ADRC cohort and tested them in the BioFINDER-2 cohort ( Supplementary Methods [this file] ). Given that the CSF biomarkers were measured using two different FDA-approved assays in the two cohorts (Roche Elecsys in BioFINDER-2 and Fujirebio Lumipulse in Knight ADRC), we derived the CSF biomarker cutoffs for the Roche Elecsys assay in a third independent cohort from UCSF ( Supplementary Methods [this file] ), following the same approach.

A subset of 715 participants (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ) also had available plasma t-tau. 
We first investigated plasma NTA-tau concentrations across clinical diagnosis groups in BioFINDER-2 (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] A and Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
BioFINDER-2 participants were also stratified into AT groups according to the presence/absence Aβ pathology (A, determined by CSF Aβ42/40) and tau pathology (T, determined by tau-PET, Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). Plasma NTA-tau increased progressively across the AD : A modest yet significant increase in plasma NTA-tau levels was observed between A-T- and A+T- ( = 0.022, Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] B and Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). 
Additionally, we examined the levels of plasma NTA-tau across BioFINDER-2 participants stratified by Braak stages (Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). Plasma NTA-tau showed a moderate increase from Braak 0 to I-II ( = 0.016, Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] C and Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). Plasma NTA-tau was increased in PET stages positive for both Aβ and tau-PET, that is A+MTL+ N-, A+MTL+N+ and A+MTL+N+ + ( < 0.001, for all), with the latter group clearly displaying the highest NTA-tau concentrations (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] and Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). 
Plasma NTA-tau levels were also significantly higher in CU+ and MCI+ compared with both CU- and nonAD- cases ( < 0.001, for all, Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). 
Models including an interaction between plasma NTA-tau levels and Aβ-status were selected as being statistically better (Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). 
In BioFINDER-2 participants, where all three imaging modalities were available, we repeated these same analyses regionally and we compared it with the other plasma biomarkers (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). 
We observed that the proportion of variation explained for plasma NTA-tau by tau was significantly higher (partial R = 0.15, 52.9% of the total R ), than by Aβ, which was minimal (partial R = 0.01, 4.3% of the total R , difference: < 0.001, Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] B and Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ), supporting the results of the previous analysis. Within this subset, plasma NTA-tau was again mostly explained by tau (partial R = 0.16, 54.4% of the total R ) and minimally by Aβ (partial R = 0.01, 4.4% of the total R , difference: < 0.001), whereas plasma t-tau was poorly explained by both Aβ (partial R = 0.00, 7.2% of the total R ) and tau (partial R = 0.01, 25.6% of the total R , difference: = 0.454; Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] C and Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ). 
We assessed whether baseline plasma NTA-tau levels are useful in predicting longitudinal tau-PET increases, brain atrophy and cognitive decline in participants within the AD (CU+ , MCI+ , AD+) at baseline (description in Supplementary Table 11 [this file] – 15 [this file] , respectively). 
Longitudinal measures of plasma NTA-tau were available in BioFINDER-1 participants (Supplementary Table 16 [this file] ). 
While we observed a significant association between plasma NTA-tau with Aβ-PET, tau-PET and neurodegeneration in Aβ-positive participants, our results demonstrate that plasma NTA-tau levels are strongly associated with tau pathology measured by tau-PET in Aβ-positive individuals, especially in regions known for the typical tau deposition in intermediate/late stages (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ).

Again, those CU participants at higher CSF stages (4–5) at baseline, were much more prone to progress to MCI with a HR of 16.0 (95%CI: 3.2, 81.1, p<0.001, Fig. 5E [rid=F13] - F [rid=F13] and Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ) compared to those in stage 1–3, supporting the clinical utility of the proposed staging model. 
Nonetheless, the overall behaviour of these CSF biomarkers by the biomarker stages was similar to that in the main cohort ( Fig. 6B [rid=F14] and Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). Aβ-PET was once again the first modality to cross the 1.96SD threshold at CSF stage 1 (Aβ42/Ab40 stage), followed by tau-PET in CSF stage 3 (pT205/T205 stage) and, finally, CSF NfL crossing this threshold at the final stage (total-tau stage; Fig. 6C [rid=F14] and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). Details of participants characteristics ( Ext Data Fig. 2 [rid=F2] ), tau-PET binding in different regions ( Ext Data Figure 4 [rid=F4] and Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ) and other cognitive measures ( Ext Data Figure 5 [rid=F5] and Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ) per CSF stage can be found in the Ext Data. Stability analyses, within participants with available longitudinal CSF measures (n=51, Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ), also showed that most participants remained at the same stage (n=46, 90.2%) or progressed (n=4, 7.8%) at follow-up ( Ext Data Fig. 3C [rid=F3] - D [rid=F3] ). 
As in the case of BioFINDER-2, CSF stage 2 (pT217/T217 stage) was optimal for predicting Aβ-PET positivity (AUC[95%CI]=0.89[0.85, 0.94], Fig. 6D [rid=F14] & G [rid=F14] and Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ), whereas CSF stage 4 (MTBR-tau243 stage) was optimal for predicting tau-PET positivity (AUC[95%CI]=0.94[0.91, 0.96], Fig. 6E [rid=F14] & H [rid=F14] ). Consistent with findings in BioFINDER-2, higher CSF stages were predictive of more advanced A/T stages, as assessed by PET (c-index[95%CI]=0.89[0.86, 0.92], Fig. 6 F [rid=F14] & I [rid=F14] , Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
We found that CU (CDR=0) and very mild AD (CDR=0.5) participants at the highest CSF stages (4–5; MTBR-tau243 and total-tau stages) exhibited an increased risk (HR[95%CI]=6.9[3.0, 16.0], p<0.001) of progressing to AD dementia (CDR≥1) at follow-up, even when adjusting for age, sex and clinical status ( , CDR=0 or CDR=0.5) at baseline, compared to participants at CSF stages 1–3 ( Fig. 6J [rid=F14] - K [rid=F14] and Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). Similarly, CU participants at higher CSF stages ( , 4–5) had higher risk (HR[95%CI]=4.2[2.0, 8.8], p<0.001) of progressing to very mild AD or more advanced disease stages when compared to participants at lower, but positive, CSF stages (1–3, Fig. 6L [rid=F14] - M [rid=F14] and Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ).

As preliminary data using [ F]GTP-1 has shown greater sensitivity to longitudinal change in tau PET using , defined as the number of voxels above a defined threshold divided by the total number of voxels in that region (ie, the percentage of abnormal voxels within a given region), in the temporal meta-ROI, we compared sample size reduction using annual percentage change in tau extent and SUVR for [ F]RO948 in this region (eMethods 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Inclusion and exclusion criteria are described elsewhere ; Aβ-status was determined using amyloid-PET (AVID 05e and Expedition-3, [ F]florbetapir; ADNI, [ F]florbetaben or [ F]florbetapir; BioFINDER, [ F]flutemetamol) and neocortical composite cutoffs (eMethods 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Annual change in SUVR [(follow-up SUVR − baseline SUVR) / change in time] is reported in eTables 4 to 7 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
In Aβ-positive individuals with MCI, the greatest change was seen in DDS II (temporal cortical regions: 5.82%; 95% CI, 4.67%-6.97%; < .001) ( Figure 4 [rid=noi230023f4] A), whereas in individuals with AD dementia, the greatest change was seen in stage III (parietal regions: 7.47%; 95% CI, 6.18%-8.78%; < .001) ( Figure 4 [rid=noi230023f4] A; eTables 4 and 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Findings from 1-sample tests are included in the eTables 4, 5, 6, and 7 in Supplement 1 [this file] . Findings using Braak ROIs were similar to those using DDSs (eTables 6 and 7 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Across both data-driven and Braak ROIs, variation in the number of tau-positive ROIs decreased across clinical groups (eTable 8 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). However, significance levels varied by ROI and disease stage (eTable 9 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Using individualized ROIs, the highest tau-PET–positive DDS approach performed best across diagnostic groups (Aβ-positive CU, 6.69%; 95% CI, 5.83%- 7.55%; < .001; Aβ-positive MCI, 8.67%; 95% CI, 7.49%-9.85%; < .001; AD dementia, 10.74%; 95% CI, 9.33%-12.20%; < .001) (eTable 9 in Supplement 1 [this file] ), even when using an alternative reference region combining the cerebellum, brainstem, and eroded subcortical white matter (eFigure in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Sample size estimations (ie, the number of participants required per arm to detect an intervention effect) assuming hypothetical intervention effects of 20%, 30%, and 40% are included in eTables 10, 11, and 12 in the Supplement [this file] . 
When performing a sensitivity analysis comparing annual percentage change in tau extent and [ F]RO948 SUVR in the temporal meta-ROI in a simulated intervention that reduced longitudinal tau accumulation by 30%, sample sizes were consistently lower for SUVR (Aβ-positive CU, 17.90%; 95% CI, 11.47%-24.33%; = .007; Aβ-positive MCI, 29.47%; 95% CI, 19.55%-39.39%; = .003; AD dementia, 33.94%; 95% CI, 25.02%-42.86%; < .001) (eTable 13 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Among the 406 participants (137 Aβ-positive CU, 144 Aβ-positive MCI, and 41 AD dementia) with longitudinal [ F]flortaucipir tau PET, the mean (SD) age was 77.18 (7.74) years, and 41 were female (48.32%) (eTable 14 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Further, individualized ROIs resulted in significantly higher estimates of annual percentage change compared with group-level ROIs, with the highest tau-PET–positive DDS approach performed best across diagnostic groups (eTables 15 and 16 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Similar to [ F]RO948, sample size reductions were greater using individualized ROIs compared with group-level ROIs, with highest tau-PET–positive DDS performing best (eTables 19, 20, and 21 in Supplement 1 [this file] ).

For the RADC cohort, global cognition closest to death was estimated using a -score, based on the mean and standard deviation of the combined cohorts baseline visit, average of 19 tests from five cognitive domains ( Supplementary material [this file] ). Episodic memory closest to death was estimated in the same manner with seven tests ( Supplementary material [this file] ). 
Demographics of the cohort with cognitively unimpaired older adults ( = 545, 53% female, mean age 65, mean education 13 years, 49% -ɛ4 carriers), the Aβ− subgroup ( = 418, 52% female, mean age 61, mean education 13 years, 42% -ɛ4 carriers; Table 1 [rid=awad135-T1] ) and of the neuropathological dataset ( = 639, mean age 87.4 ± 7.00, 33% female, mean education 16 years) can be found in Table 1 [rid=awad135-T1] and Supplementary Tables 1 and 2 [this file] . 
To examine if these associations are independent of Aβ, we adjusted the age and regional tau-PET associations for regional Aβ-PET signal ( Fig. 2B [rid=awad135-F2] and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). Mediation models show similar results ( Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). 
In the neuropathological dataset, age and tau tangle score were positively associated for all regions except lateral occipital tau tangles ( Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ; = 0.10–0.39, = 0.020–<0.001). 
In the next step we investigated the associations of tau-PET SUVR with regional volume and ROI thickness, while adjusting for sex, regional Aβ-PET, and the off-target variable ( Fig. 3A [rid=awad135-F3] and for details see Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). 
In the Aβ− subgroup, higher ERC/BA35 tau-PET was significantly associated with lower volume in subiculum ( = −0.23, < 0.001) and CA1 ( = −0.18, = 0.003), and lower BA35 ( = −0.30, < 0.001) and ERC ( = −0.12, < 0.001) thickness; higher precuneus/posterior cingulate tau-PET was associated with reduced thickness in that region ( = −0.19, < 0.001; Fig. 3 [rid=awad135-F3] and Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ), again adjusting for Aβ-PET and sex. 
In the whole sample of cognitively unimpaired older adults, significant associations with global cognition (mPACC5) and episodic memory were found for higher age, ERC/BA35 tau-PET, subiculum and CA1 volume, and BA35, inferior temporal, and precuneus/posterior cingulate thickness (see Supplementary Table 8 [this file] for details). 
Imaging measures in other regions were not associated with the cognition measures ( Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). 
Higher ERC/BA35 and precuneus/posterior cingulate tau-PET were significantly associated with reduced global cognition ( Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). 
In the full neuropathological cohort of cognitively unimpaired older adults, age was associated with global cognition ( = −0.17, < 0.001; Supplementary Table 9 [this file] and Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). Tau load in temporal regions partially mediated the age-global cognition association ( Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ; variance explained: 12–29%). 
In the Aβ− subgroup, only higher ERC tau load was associated with reduced episodic memory ( = −0.20, = 0.021; Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). 
I , the results remained consistent even when excluding individuals with high meningeal/skull tau-PET binding ( Supplementary Tables 1–9 [this file] ), using robust regression models (data not shown) or additionally adjusting the analyses for -ɛ4 carriership (data not shown), and when using CSF Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio instead of regional Aβ-PET as a covariate ( Supplementary Tables 1–9 [this file] ). Results further converged with the primary analyses when using global instead of regional Aβ-PET as a covariate for Pearson partial correlations and mediation models (age-thickness/volume associations: Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ; age-cognition associations: mPACC5: = −0.03, 95% CI: −0.04:−0.01, = 0.010, 8%; ADAS: = −0.03, 95% CI: −0.05:−0.01, = 0.015, 9%). Note that age-tau associations in the Aβ− subgroup yielded slightly stronger results ( Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). Finally, tau-PET measures were significantly associated with CSF p-tau181 for all but the motor region in the whole sample and for temporal and frontal regions in the Aβ− subgroup ( Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
No association between the tau-PET signal in the parietal regions and cognition were found, which could reflect lower levels of tau compared to ERC/BA35 tau-PET ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ) or a relative recent aggregation of tau and, thus, has not exerted an effect on cognition yet.

They also provided better ΔAIC-values as compared to the best single predictor tau-PET ( Supplementary Tables 2 [this file] and 3 [this file] ). 
In a sensitivity analysis, when restricting the analysis to only amnestic MCI participants (n=90), we found similar results ( Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). Further, when including only participants that were Aβ-positive ( Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ) to mimic the scenario of a clinical trial, tau-PET and baseline cognition were significant predictors, while NfL and cortical atrophy were no longer significant predictors. Finally, when using change in modified PACC over time as the cognitive outcome (instead of change in MMSE), we again found that tau-PET and baseline cognition were the strongest predictors of cognitive decline in the parsimonious models, but with minor contributions from plasma NfL and plasma p-tau217 ( Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
We found that tau-PET and baseline cognition were again the best predictors for longitudinal cognitive decline, but plasma NfL and cortical atrophy did not contribute to the model ( Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). 
We found that using the parsimonious models defined in BioFINDER-2, i.e. tau-PET, baseline cognition, NfL and cortical thickness, to enrich for higher risk of cognitive decline resulted in significant reduction in group sizes with preserved statistical power ( Figure 2 [rid=F2] and Supplementary Figure 1 [this file] ; full details provided in Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). There were no statistically significant differences in the reduced group sizes between using CSF or plasma biomarkers ( Supplementary Figure 1 [this file] ). In a sensitivity analysis, a more simple model only containing the most important predictors (that is: tau-PET and cognition) performed similarly to the full models for study enrichment ( Supplementary Figure 2 [this file] ). 
Further, baseline cognition (here evaluated using composites of memory and executive function) showed an association with future cognitive decline even after adjusting for baseline MMSE, but performed significantly inferior compared to the parsimonious model or tau-PET when used alone ( Table 2 [rid=T2] , Supplementary tables 2 [this file] and 3 [this file] ). 
Restricting the study population using the parsimonious model to more pathological biomarker values resulted in a significant reduction in sample sizes needed ( Figure 2 [rid=F2] ; Supplementary Table 8 [this file] and Supplementary Figure 1 [this file] ).

Details of the assessments are presented in Supplemental Methods 2 [this file] . 
Other outcomes used for interim analysis are detailed in Supplemental Methods 4 [this file] . 
Other secondary endpoints were: (i) DIAN-TU Cognitive Composite ( Supplemental Method 3 [this file] ), with lower scores interpreted as worse performance; (ii) Functional Assessment Scale (FAS), which measures the participant’s ability to perform daily activities, with higher scores indicating worse performance; (iii) MMSE with lower scores indicate worse performance. 
Surveillance MRI was built into the dose escalation design to monitor for ARIA events routinely, and any suspected ARIA was assessed by the medical monitoring team promptly (see Supplemental Figure 1 [this file] ). 
For the final analysis, the primary analysis was performed for the OLE modified intent-to-treat (mITT) population, defined as participants who received any gantenerumab treatment post-OLE baseline, had at least one PiB-PET SUVR assessment prior to gantenerumab treatment, and a post-baseline assessment (based on OLE period data only, referred to as “OLE only Gant”, Supplementary Figure 5C [this file] ). We estimated annual dropout rates of 5% and 10% and anticipated approximately 56 to 43 participants to remain at the end of the 3-year OLE, and the study was predicted to have over 99% power to detect the projected mean change from baseline using a one-sided one-sample t-test with a type I error rate of 2.5% (see Supplemental Methods 2 [this file] ). 
The primary analysis for the key secondary endpoint of time to recurrent progression in CDR-SB, involved comparing participants who were treated with gantenerumab in either the double-blind or OLE period (referred to as “Any Gant”, Supplementary Figure 5A [this file] ) to the main set controls. For all the comparisons using the Cox model stated below, start time was the baseline for the corresponding population as defined in Supplementary Figure 5A [this file] – C [this file] , end time was the last available CDR assessment time. The same Cox proportional hazard models were also applied to the comparison (i) between the longest gantenerumab mITT Population (“Longest Gant”, Supplementary Figure 5B [this file] ) and the main set of controls, (ii) between Longest Gant mITT Population and the extended set of controls, (iii) between OLE only Gant mITT Population and the main set of control. Post-hoc sensitivity analyses based on CDR are described in Supplemental Method 1 [this file] . 
The detailed steps for calculating CentiMarker are described in Supplemental Method 6 [this file] . 
For the interim analysis, the same MMRM and Cox models as described for the final analysis were used for amyloid PET SUVR, CDR SB and global (see Supplementary Method 4 [this file] for details). 
Other methods descriptions, including assessments, imaging and fluid biomarker methods are in Supplemental Methods 2 [this file] . 
For CDR analysis based on baseline asymptomatic participants (double-blind baseline for prior gantenerumab treated group and OLE baseline for prior placebo and solanezumab treated group), the Any Gant mITT population ( Supplementary Figure 5A [this file] ) included 53 participants, the Longest Gant treated mITT population ( Supplementary Figure 5B [this file] ) included 22 participants, the OLE only Gant treated mITT population included 40 participants ( Supplementary Figure 5C [this file] ), the main set of control group included 74 participants, and the extended control group ( Supplementary Figure 5B [this file] ) that included the OLE baseline measures, comprised 86 participants. Length of follow up for different groups are presented in Supplemental Table 1 [this file] . 
For the OLE period, the OLE only Gant baseline asymptomatic group with average duration of 2 years (n=40), the hazard ratio (95% CI) was 1.39 (0.46, 4.19) for CDR global and 1.41 (0.59, 3.33) for CDR-SB (see Supplemental Table 2 [this file] ). Amyloid-plaque removal, measured by PiB-PET SUVR, was dose-dependent, with approximately 3-fold greater rates of amyloid-plaque lowering by tripling the dose used in the double-blind period ( Supplemental Figure 2 [this file] ). 
The adjusted mean change from OLE baseline (mean 2.62, SD 1.30) to year 3 (mean 1.96, SD 1.12) was PiB-PET SUVR of −0.71 (95% CI −0.88 to −0.53, p < 0.0001, Supplemental Figure 3 [this file] , shown in Centiloids in Figure 2A [rid=F2] ). Significant reductions were also observed in PiB-PET SUVR from OLE baseline to the end of OLE year 1 (−0.12, 95% CI −0.21 to −0.03, p = 0.012) and OLE year 2 (−0.47, 95% CI −0.60 to −0.33, p<0.0001) ( Supplemental Figure 3 [this file] ). Participants who received higher doses of gantenerumab (1020–1500 mg every 2 weeks) showed approximately 3-fold greater rates of amyloid plaque lowering, with annual reduction of 0.35 SUVR (OLE year 1 to 2) compared to those on lower doses (225 mg every 4 weeks), with annual reduction of 0.06 SUVR ( Supplemental Figure 2 [this file] ). At the end of the OLE, 8 (15%) participants remained amyloid PET normal (defined by SUVR<1.25) , 8 (15%) participants converted from abnormal to normal, and 38 (70%) participants remained amyloid PET abnormal ( Supplemental Table 8 [this file] ). 
At OLE year 3, a significant reduction in mean SUVR relative to the double-blind baseline was demonstrated for OLE participants from the gantenerumab treated arm (−0.44, 95% CI −0.76 to −0.12) and solanezumab treated arm (−0.47, 95% CI −0.86, −0.09), but not for OLE participants from the placebo arm (−0.07, 95% CI −0.51, 0.36) ( Supplemental Figure 3 [this file] ). 
In 53 participants who were asymptomatic at baseline and were included in Any Gant, the hazard ratio (95% CI) of time to first progression in CDR global score for treatment group vs. the main set of control was 0.84 (0.40 to 1.77), and the hazard ratio for time to recurrent progression in CDR-SB was 0.83 (0.50 to 1.36) ( Figure 3 [rid=F3] , Supplemental Table 3 [this file] ). 
When comparing the treatment group with the extended control group (n = 86), the hazard ratio (95% CI) is 0.40 (0.14 to 1.16) for time to first progression in CDR global and 0.53 (0.29 to 0.97) for time to recurrent progression in CDR-SB ( Figure 3 [rid=F3] , Supplemental Table 3 [this file] ). For each population, the number and percentage of censored participants and reasons for censoring are presented in Supplemental Table 4 [this file] . Sensitivity analyses conducted either by excluding double-blind placebo arm participants who did not enroll in OLE from the main set of control or by using control participants matched by baseline EYO, length of follow-up and mutation type, resulted in similar hazard ratios ( Supplemental Table 5 [this file] ). 
Change from baseline in original scale were provided in Supplemental Table 9 [this file] . 
Table 3 [rid=T3] and Supplemental Table 6 [this file] summarizes the incidence of TEAEs, which were greater than 10% in the OLE period. Treatment-emergent serious adverse events (SAEs) and adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation are detailed in Table 3 [rid=T3] and Supplemental Table 6 [this file] , summarized by system organ class and preferred terms. 
Even at this dose, amyloid plaques were not fully cleared in 70% of participants after one year of dose titration and one year at maximum doses, though there was substantial progress toward amyloid removal (most with Centiloid <25, supplemental figure 6 [this file] ) with an acceptable safety profile. 
To date, all trials in mutation carriers have predicted outcomes in late-onset SAD (see Supplemental Table 7 [this file] ), and so an open question is whether these findings will be replicated in ongoing prevention trials of SAD that remove plaques.

For tau PET composite SUVR, participants in the amyloid‐no‐change class exhibited slower rates of annual change compared to those in the amyloid‐reduction class who, in turn, demonstrated slower rates than those in the amyloid‐growth class (Table S1 [this file] in supporting information). Similar patterns were observed for MRI hippocampal volumes and MRI precuneus thickness although the differences between the amyloid‐reduction class and the amyloid‐growth class were much smaller (Table S1 [this file] ). Conversely, for FDG‐PET composite SUVR, both the amyloid‐reduction class and the amyloid‐growth class exhibited comparable rates of decline (Table S1 [this file] ). 
A sensitivity analysis was conducted, excluding the single placebo participant who was classified into the amyloid‐reduction class, and the results were found to be consistent (Figure S1 [this file] ). 
Figures 2 [rid=alz13735-fig-0002] and S2 [this file] in supporting information display the estimated annual rates of change for clinical and cognitive outcomes. Despite having similar baseline characteristics, the amyloid‐reduction class exhibited a reduction in the annual decline rate compared to the amyloid‐growth class across multiple measures: CDR‐SB decline was reduced by 47.1%, MMSE by 31.8%, Digit Symbol by 48.2%, ISLT by 56.3%, and FAS by 40.3% (Table S2 [this file] in supporting information).
