We employed Personalized-HMM to identify disease-related states with their transitions, and the 5-fold cross-validation on the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort resulted in a ten-state model ( Figures 1 [rid=fig1] A and 1B, Table S8 [this file] ) as well as a transition matrix ( Table 1 [rid=tbl1] ). Each state was primarily differentiated by the demographics (age, sex, education), genetics (Apolipoprotein E4 alleles, APOE4), cognitive function scores (MMSE, CDRSB, ADAS, and so forth) and atrophy brain regions (hippocampus, fusiform, entorhinal, and so forth) ( Figure 1 [rid=fig1] C; Figures S6–S8 [this file] ). 
These disease-related states were highly reproducible when we trained the model on participants who were Abeta-positive in the ADNI dataset ( Figure S10 [this file] ). 
We analyzed the correlations between the identified disease-related states and Abeta/pTau measures ( Figures 2 [rid=fig2] A and 2B, Tables S9 [this file] and S10 [this file] ): (i) Most of CN participants (including those with negative Abeta status (A-), positive Abeta status (A+), negative pTau status (T-), and positive pTau status (T+)) were expressed in the states A-I, A-II, and B-I. (2) A-II, A-III, B-I, and B-II corresponded to a large number of cognitively impaired but nondemented participants with A- or T-; and MCI participants with A+ or T+ mainly concentrated in the states A-III, A-IV, B-II, and C-I. (3) There were a comparable number of participants with AD dementia and labeled with C-I and C-II, who had similar distributions in amyloid status, predominately A+ (46.51% and 57.26%) and T+ (42.64% and 43.55%); participants within states C-III and C-IV were mostly A+ (91.91%, 100.00%) and T+ (79.77%, 87.10%) ( Tables S9 [this file] and S10 [this file] ). Participants with A+T+ tended to have more severe neurodegeneration than those with A+T-, as expected ( Figure 2 [rid=fig2] D and Table S11 [this file] ). 
The significant differences between the states of stage A and stage B were revealed in terms of cognitive score and core brain regions ( Figure S9 [this file] ). 
We identified disease-related states of each stage ( Figures S11–S13 [this file] ) compared to healthy controls. Participants progressing to stage C had accelerated atrophy rates in almost all selected regions, especially in the middle, inferior temporal lobe, hippocampus, and cingulate gyrus ( Figure 3 [rid=fig3] B and Figure S13 [this file] ). 
Regarding cognitive deterioration, participants with positive Abeta (A+) or pTau (T+) in stage A had an average more rapid decline over time than those in stage B ( Table 2 [rid=tbl2] ; Figures 4 [rid=fig4] C–4F), but the deterioration trend forparticipants in stage A was non-linear and accelerated once these participants turned into state A-IV ( Figure S11 [this file] ). Participants in stage C have significantly worse cognitive abilities than those in stages A and B ( Figure S14 [this file] ). 
Regarding the progression from any state to the final C-IV state or AD dementia ( Figures S15 [this file] and S16 [this file] ), Kaplan-Meier analysis revealed that participants in states A-III or B-II had only a 25% risk of conversion to the terminal state C-IV within 96 months ( Figure S15 [this file] ). Intuitively, Kaplan-Meier curves of time to conversion to AD dementia show that participants in states of stage A or B had slow progression rates to AD dementia ( Figure S16 [this file] ). 
Similar findings were observed in the AIBL dataset ( Tables S12 [this file] and S13 [this file] , Figures 5 [rid=fig5] C and 5D; Figures S17–S19 [this file] ). Moreover, our model’s performance is substantiated by the results from the C-Index and ROC curves ( Table S14 [this file] and Figure S20 [this file] ), consistently highlighting its exceptional predictive capability compared to conventional machine learning approaches. Our model utilized identified disease states as predictive biomarkers for AD progression, maintaining stable predictive performance across both balanced and imbalanced populations, with improved performance observed in the imbalanced group ( Table S15 [this file] and Figure S21 [this file] ). 
The three non-overlapping stages had different trends in cognitive scores and the ratios of brain sub-regions over time ( Figure S14 [this file] ).

To determine whether the relationship between sleep duration and brain Aβ accumulation reflected a U‐shaped curve, as is reported for sleep and cognition, we analyzed a categorical sleep duration variable (see Table 2 [rid=dad212579-tbl-0002] , Table S2 [this file] in supporting information, and Figure 2 [rid=dad212579-fig-0002] ). For ε4 carriers (β = 4.33 ± 1.58, = 0.007), but not for the whole cohort or ε4 non‐carriers, baseline sleep duration of < 6 hours was associated with a faster rate of brain Aβ accumulation compared to optimal sleep duration of 6 to 8 hours (see Table 2 [rid=dad212579-tbl-0002] and Table S2 [this file] ). 
Analysis of categorical sleep efficiency (see Table 2 [rid=dad212579-tbl-0002] and Figure 3 [rid=dad212579-fig-0003] ) revealed that baseline sleep efficiency of < 65% was associated with faster brain Aβ accumulation over time relative to those with sleep efficiency > 85%, in the whole cohort (β = 2.91 ± 0.93, = 0.002), and in ε4 non‐carriers (β = 2.86 ± 0.89, = 0.001), but not in ε4 carriers (see Table S2 [this file] ). 
For ε4 carriers (β = 3.42 ± 1.64, = 0.038), but not for the whole cohort or ε4 non‐carriers, self‐reported “poor” sleep quality was nominally associated with a faster rate of brain Aβ accumulation compared to those reporting “very good” sleep quality (see Table S2 [this file] and Figure S1 [this file] in supporting information), after Bonferroni correction. Moreover, the intercepts of Figure S1 [this file] suggest that ε4 carriers reporting “poor” sleep quality have greater baseline brain Aβ burden compared to ε4 carriers with “very good” or “fairly good” self‐reported sleep quality, though these main effects were not significant. 
Analysis of sleep onset latency variables, both continuous and categorical, revealed no significant relationships, for any sub‐group comparison, with respect to rate of brain Aβ accumulation (see Table S2 [this file] and Figure S2 [this file] in supporting information). However, Figure S2 [this file] clearly shows that ε4 carriers with sleep onset latency of ≥ 60 minutes had higher brain Aβ levels at both baseline, and over time, compared to ε4 carriers with sleep onset latency < 60 minutes, though the rate of brain Aβ accumulation did not differ.

context_description:
The top ranked DAPs of the reduction in LRRK2 PD group were PRL, LPO, and C3 ( Fig. 1b [rid=F1] , c [rid=F1] , and Supplementary Fig. 1a [this file] , b [this file] ). 
When these features were employed to train the RandomForest model utilizing the cross-validation technique, we obtained a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) with an average area under the curve (AUC) of 0.95 (standard deviation (std) = 0.02) and a precision-recall (PR) Curve with an average AUC of 0.94 (std = 0.03) ( Fig. 1e [rid=F1] , and Supplementary Fig. 1c [this file] ). 
In the comparison of sPD vs. HC, we found 301 DAPs (35 up-regulated, 266 down-regulated) (Supplementary Table 3), in which immune response pathway was enriched, while synapse related pathways were reduced ( Fig. 1f [rid=F1] , g [rid=F1] , and Supplementary Fig. 1d [this file] ). The top feature proteins identified by OmicLearn also showed a strong overlap with DAPs, achieving a ROC with an average AUC of 0.72 (std = 0.04) and a PR Curve with an average AUC of 0.82 (std = 0.03) ( Fig. 1h [rid=F1] , i [rid=F1] , and Supplementary Fig. 1e [this file] ). 
Comparing LRRK2 PD vs. sPD, we found 168 DAPs (136 up-regulated, 32 down-regulated) (Supplementary Table 4), which were enriched in lysosomal (GRN, CTSB, TMEM106A, and GAA) and immune (C1QTNF1, GPNMB, and HLA-DQA2) pathways ( Fig. 1j [rid=F1] , Supplementary Fig. 1f [this file] , g [this file] ). In both the above comparisons, we observed enriched pathways of immune response and RNA localization, whereas PRL and WIF1 were the top proteins of reduction ( Supplementary Fig. 1h [this file] – k [this file] ). 
Only 11 DAPs were detected in comparing LRRK2 PD vs. ProLRRK2 PD (0 up-regulated, 11 down-regulated) (Supplementary Table 7), with PRL, LPO, and VIP as top ranked ( Supplementary Fig. 2a [this file] ). The analysis of GBA PD vs. proGBA PD also identified a small number of DAPs (10 DAPs, 2 upregulated, 8 downregulated) (Supplementary Table 8), with PRL and LPO as overlapping proteins between the two studies ( Supplementary Fig. 2b [this file] ). 
Again, we did not detect any significant DAPs comparing SAA− and SAA+ subgroups in the LRRK2 PD ( Supplementary Fig. 2c [this file] ) (Supplementary Table 9). 
Similarly, extracellular matrix proteins such as EFEMP1, APOE, FN1, CHI3L, TGFBI, and FBLN5 showed comparable levels between the prodromal and HC groups but declined over time in the LRRK2 PD group ( Fig. 2a [rid=F2] – c [rid=F2] and Supplementary Fig. 3a [this file] ) (Supplementary Table 11). 
Instead, alterations were detected in lipid transport (APOC1, APOC2, APOC3) and acute phase proteins (SERPINA3, SERPINA6, and SERPING1) during the prodromal or PD phases ( Supplementary Fig. 3b [this file] – d [this file] ) (Supplementary Table 13). 
A similar increase was also observed for Cathepsin D in the medium of astrocytes ( Supplementary Fig. 4a [this file] , b [this file] ). LDH activity in the culture medium did not differ between groups, confirming lack of cytotoxicity ( Supplementary Fig. 4c [this file] – e [this file] ). Furthermore, proteinase K treatment reduced the amount of Cathepsin B in the medium, and the combined treatment with detergent and proteinase K did not result in further reduction ( Supplementary Fig. 4f [this file] , g [this file] ), suggesting that the secreted lysosomal enzyme is present predominantly in a unencapsulated form. 
We next analyzed urine proteomics data (PPMI) from human LRRK2 PD vs. HC and observed the enrichment of lysosome lumen pathway (TMEM106B, CTSO, CTSZ, and GBA) and glycolipid metabolic process (GLB1, FUCA1, NAGA, SMPD1, and GM2A); in contrast, the immune response pathway (WFDC2, CD59, CD83, DEFB1, and FCER2) was decreased ( Fig. 4a [rid=F4] , b [rid=F4] and Supplementary Fig. 5a [this file] , b [this file] ) (Supplementary Table 14). The identified feature proteins by OmicLeran showed a strong overlap with the DAPs, achieving a ROC with an average AUC of 0.92 (std = 0.03) and a PR Curve with an average AUC of 0.94 (std = 0.03) ( Fig. 4c [rid=F4] , d [rid=F4] , and Supplementary Fig. 5c [this file] ). Comparing the urine proteomics of LRRK2 PD vs. sPD, we observed similar patterns of elevated lysosome lumen and glycolipid catabolic pathways in LRRK2 PD ( Fig. 4e [rid=F4] , f [rid=F4] , and Supplementary Fig. 5d [this file] , e [this file] ) (Supplementary Table 15). The analysis of urine data of LRRK2 PD vs. Pro LRRK2 PD identified only a few DAPs, including HBD, HBB, HBA1, AKR1B1, SFRP1, and SDSL ( Supplementary Fig. 5f [this file] – g [this file] ) (Supplementary Table 16). No DAPs were observed in the analysis of LRRK2 PD SAA+ vs. LRRK2 PD SAA− subgroups ( Supplementary Fig. 5h [this file] ) (Supplementary Table 17). 
Surprisingly, the above comparisons revealed no significant DAPs, due to the same stringent threshold used in our CSF data (FDR and 1.5*SD) ( Supplementary Fig. 5i [this file] – l [this file] ). 
Moreover, M1 is enriched in endosome and vesicle pathways and M2 is enriched in GTPase motor activity and NAD binding ( Supplementary Fig. 6a [this file] , b [this file] ). 
Lysosome lumen, lysosomal membrane, sphingolipid metabolic process, glycolipid catabolic process, and glycosphingolipid catabolic process were significantly enriched in M10 through GO term analysis ( Fig. 5 e [rid=F5] – g [rid=F5] and Supplementary Fig. 6c [this file] ). Similar to the M1 and M2 in CSF, the M5 and M8 from urine dataset were enriched in vesicle lumen and secretory granule lumen, ATP hydrolysis activity and GTP binding, respectively ( Supplementary Fig. 6d [this file] , e [this file] ). 
Among these, MAN2B2, IDS, and CTSB displayed the highest positive correlation coefficients ( Supplementary Fig. 6f [this file] , g [this file] ) (Supplementary Table 24). 
The GO analysis indicated an increase in mitochondrial matrix and multiple catabolic processes pathways as well as a decrease in translation at pre-/post-synapse (RPL10a, RPL27, RPL26, RPL4, RPL13, RPL8, PRS14, PRS15A, and PRS11) ( Supplementary Fig. 7a [this file] – c [this file] ). In contrast, analysis of urine samples from vs. WT mice showed 54 DAPs (17 up-regulated, 39 down-regulated, FDR < 0.05) (Supplementary Table 26) with a significant decrease in the lysosomal lumen (TMEM106B, CTSA, CTSH, PLD3, and GUSB), glycosphingolipid (GSLs) and catabolism (GLB1, GALC, and NEU1) pathways ( Fig. 6a [rid=F6] , b [rid=F6] , Supplementary Fig. 7d [this file] , e [this file] ), consistent with a role of mouse Lrrk2 in promoting the secretion of lysosomal proteins . 
We crossed a human BAC- transgenic line to mice to generate a “humanized” mutant line h ( Supplementary Fig. 8a [this file] ). The h mouse line shows comparable protein levels of human LRRK2 mutant to WT mouse LRRK2 in tissues however with remarkably elevated phosphorylation of Rab10 and Rab12 ( Supplementary Fig. 8b [this file] – f [this file] ). GO term analysis indicated that the most significantly enriched pathways were lysosomal lumen (GUSB, TPP1, GAA, and CTSD) and glycosphingolipid biosynthesis (GALC, GLB1, GBA1, and HEXB), followed by dendrite cytoplasm and proteoglycan catabolic process ( Fig. 6c [rid=F6] , d [rid=F6] , and Supplementary Fig. 8g [this file] , h [this file] ). Moreover, when analyzing samples from h vs. mice through stringent analysis (FDR < 0.05), we observed 106 DAPs (60 up-regulated, 46 down-regulated) (Supplementary Table 28), of which lysosomal lumen (TMEM106B, CTSA, CTSD, PLD3, and GUSB) and glycosphingolipid biosynthesis (GLB1, CALC, GBA1, and HEXB) pathways were the top ranked enriched pathways, followed by membrane raft, pore complex, vacuole organization, and membrane lipid catabolic process ( Fig. 6e [rid=F6] , f [rid=F6] , Supplementary Fig. 8i [this file] , j [this file] ). 
GO term analysis further verified the enrichment in lysosome lumen, lysosome membrane, membrane lipid catabolic process, glycolipid catabolic process, and glycosphingolipid catabolic process pathways, which were similar to the human urine M10 module ( Fig. 5e [rid=F5] – g [rid=F5] , Fig. 6g [rid=F6] – i [rid=F6] , and Supplementary Fig. 9a [this file] ). 
Proteins associated with these pathways were elevated in the urine of h compared to WT or mice, and in the CSF and urine of LRRK2 PD patients compared to HC, whereas they were decreased in the urine of mice compared to WT(z-score > 2 or < −2) ( Supplementary Fig. 9b [this file] ) (Supplementary Table 30). In the Upstream Analysis, transcription factor EB (TFEB) was top ranked, showing similar patterns across all comparisons ( Supplementary Fig. 9b [this file] , c [this file] ) (Supplementary Table 31). 
Notably, this model exhibits robust kinase activity ( Supplementary Fig. 8c [this file] – f [this file] ), leading to enhanced phosphorylation of Rab10 and Rab12, consistent with the phospho-Rab profiles reported in the brains of LRRK2 PD with tau pathology . 
We then downloaded the top 10 canonical and upstream regulator results and plotted the results with a R package “heatmap” (ref), shown as Supplementary Fig. 9b [this file] , c [this file] .

The demographic characteristics of each cohort are presented in Supplementary Table 1 [this file] . The characteristics of our CNV analysis are shown in Supplementary Table 2 [this file] . 
We screened a subset of samples from one COURAGE-PD site (Gasser/Sharma study; see Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ) using the multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) assay. 
Upon closer examination of CNV carrier distribution across the genome-wide significant regions identified through Fisher’s exact test and/or logistic regression, we observed a striking overrepresentation of samples from a single sub-cohort, namely the Gasser/Sharma study from Tuebingen (see Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
These analyses revealed that the strongest genome-wide signals were almost entirely driven by samples from the Tuebingen sub-cohort ( Supplementary Figure 1 [this file] ). 
After multiple testing correction and fine-mapping, we identified six genome-wide significant CNV loci associated with PD ( Supplementary Figure 2.A [this file] ). However, these loci were no longer significant when the Tuebingen cohort was excluded from the analysis, replicating the inflation pattern observed with the full Neurochip array ( Supplementary Figure 2.B [this file] ). 
Indeed, among the 229 individuals carrying CNVs in PD-related genes, 91.7% were carriers of CNVs (summarised in Supplementary Table 3 [this file] and detailed in Supplementary Table 4 [rid=SD2] ). All these CNVs mostly consisted of one-copy duplications or duplications, except for seven homozygous deletions in PD patients ( Table S3 [this file] – 4 [rid=SD2] ). CNVs in were identified in 135 PD patients (115 exonic and 36 intronic, representing 1.2% of the total patients) and 75 controls (56 exonic and 22 intronic, representing 0.8% of controls, Table S3 [this file] – 4 [rid=SD2] ). 
The enrichment was significant for CNVs overlapping PD-associated genes, including , and remained consistent when the analysis was restricted to exonic CNVs ( Supplementary Figure 3 [this file] ). 
The complete list of GP2 members is provided supplementary table 5 [this file] . 
Genome-wide CNV association summary statistics are available in the Supplementary Data [this file] .

For the 23andMe dataset, the diagnosis of PD was self-reported (see Supplementary Materials [this file] ). As of 2022, E&I Review Services is part of Salus IRB ( https://www.versiticlinicaltrials.org/salusirb (https://www.versiticlinicaltrials.org/salusirb) ; Supplementary Methods [this file] ). 
For additional information, please see the Supplementary Materials [this file] . 
The PCs were fit on the set of overlapping SNPs between the datasets and the reference panels before being transformed by UMAP to represent the population substructure (see Supplementary Materials [this file] ). 
Fine-mapping analyses were conducted using the R package coloc ( https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=coloc (https://cran.r-project.org/package=coloc) ; Supplementary Methods [this file] ). 
Short-read WGS DNA sequencing was performed by Psomagen (detailed in Supplementary Methods [this file] ). 
Additional details are described in Supplementary Methods [this file] . 
Here, we performed a GWAS meta-analysis ( Figure 2 [rid=F2] ) of the African ( Supplementary Figure 4 [this file] ) and African admixed datasets ( Supplementary Figure 5 [this file] ), totaling 1,488 cases and 196,430 controls. 
Linear regression analyses in 711 African ancestry cases and 185 African admixed ancestry cases showed that rs3115534-G is also an AAO disease modifier (African ancestry: BETA =−2.004, SE = 0.57, P = 0.0005; African-admixed: BETA = −4.15, SE =0.58, P =0.015; Meta-analysis: BETA =−3.06, SE =0.40, P = 0.008) resulting in onset of PD three years earlier per risk allele ( Supplementary Figure 7 [this file] ). 
The locus in African and African admixed populations differs substantially from Europeans ( Figure 3 [rid=F3] ; Supplementary Figure 8 [this file] ), whose association with disease risk is driven by two independent signals, including rs35749011 ( -E326K) and rs76763715 ( -N370S). These variants are very rare in individuals of African and African admixed ancestry ( Supplementary Figure 14B [this file] ). Similarly, the locus considerably differs from the East Asian population, for which the rs3115534 variant was also not imputed in the largest East Asian GWAS meta-analysis ( Supplementary Figure 14C [this file] ). These differences are less noticeable when assessing the Amerindian/Latin American and indigenous populations, which harbor higher levels of African admixture ( Supplementary Figure 14D [this file] ); Loesch et al. GWAS ; rs3115534-G; OR = 1.13, 95% CI =0.41–1.86, P= 0.72; Amerindian/Latin American and indigenous 23andMe GWAS; rs3115534-G; OR = 1.56, 95% CI = 1.55–1.88, P= 0.01). 
Interestingly, the larger sub-African population haplotypes spanning the rs3115534 variant were found in the Esan and the Yoruba in Ibadan (Nigerian) populations according to 1000 Genomes ( Supplementary Figure 9 [this file] ), suggesting that this haplotype might have originated in these populations, given that founder effects result in decreased genetic admixture and therefore larger haplotype block sizes. 
Our data suggests a decreasing trend in GCase activity estimates when comparing rs3115534-GG homozygous risk allele (762.50 ± 273.50 U) versus rs3115534-GT heterozygous carriers (2743.76 ± 1960.83 U); (Welch Two Sample t-test - GG versus GT; t = −4.3138, df = 21.583, p-value = 0.00029) and rs3115534-TT homozygous non-risk allele carriers (1879.94 ± 1010.84 U) versus rs3115534-GG homozygous risk allele carrier; (Welch Two Sample t-test - GG versus TT; t = −4.7564, df = 18.363, p-value = 0.00014)( Supplementary Figures 11 [this file] and 12 [this file] ). 
Out of the 104 variants, 91 variants passed QC, imputation filters, and were present in the African and African admixed GWAS meta-analysis ( Supplementary Figure 15 [this file] ; Table 2 [rid=T2] ). 
Considering our limited sample size, we lacked statistical power to detect common genetic variants of smaller effect sizes ( Supplemental Figure 13 [this file] ). 
See appendix [this file] (p 37) for a complete list of Nigerian hospitals and institutions contributing to this cohort.

Surprisingly, our analyses revealed that proteomic features yielded better predictive performance compared to transcriptomic features in multiple machine learning algorithms (Random Forest, XGBoost, and SVM), suggesting the power of proteomic data in modeling ALS pathology (Fig. 2a [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. 1c, d [this file] ). Similarly, we applied a graph convolutional networks (GCN)-based algorithms, Multi-Omics Graph cOnvolutional NETworks (MOGONET) , for integrative analysis of both transcriptomic and proteomic data, which also showed that the proteomics features ranked top in predicting ALS and control motor neurons, compared to the transcriptomic features (Supplementary Fig. 1e [this file] ). 
The frequency of protein features selected across 10,000 training iteration models was quantified and ranked, ultimately generating a candidate list of 110 protein features ( roteomics arkers for LS 110, PMA110; Fig. 2b [rid=Fig2] , Supplementary Fig. 2a, b [this file] and Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM2] ). Incorporating other variables, such as gender, age and batch, into the machine learning-based prediction revealed that these features had only limited impact on model performance, as shown by the overlapped features with PMA110 (Supplementary Fig. 2c [this file] ). In line with previous studies , we used the top 500 most variable genes in PCA analysis and checked the distribution of these variables, but overall we didn’t find a strong biased distribution for them (Supplementary Fig. 2d, e [this file] ). Subsequent retraining using this selected PMA110 protein feature set demonstrated improved accuracy and enhanced stability in predicting ALS and control samples (Supplementary Fig. 2f [this file] ). Therefore, we utilized SHAP plots to visually evaluate the impact of PMA110 features on model predictions, considering both the feature values (encoded by gradient colors) and the direction of prediction contribution (indicating the likelihood of ALS) (Supplementary Fig. 3a [this file] ). 
We observed the expression changes for EIF4A2, ACADM, YY1 and BRD2 at the protein level, but not the RNA level (Supplementary Fig. 3b–e [this file] ), which could be explained by the marginal correlation between protein and RNA levels (Supplementary Fig. 3g [this file] ). Overall, we noticed a limited overlap among the three gene sets, suggesting the complexity of ALS pathology at different molecular regulation levels (Supplementary Fig. 3f [this file] ). To this end, we examined the PPI distance between PMA110 proteins with the ALS meta-set proteins (Supplementary Fig. 3h [this file] ). 
Notably, the hub proteins located at the central positions of each PPI cluster exhibited differential expression levels between ALS and control groups (Supplementary Fig. 4a–d [this file] ), including the well-established ALS proteins, such as TP53 and HNRNPA2B1. In addition, the interacting proteins also displayed a strong correlation of protein expression levels, further supporting the functional cooperation within each PPI cluster for ALS (Supplementary Fig. 4e–h [this file] ). 
In addition to functional and pathway enrichment analysis, we performed conservation analysis of PMA110 proteins to assess the functional significance of the candidate genes (Supplementary Fig. 5a–c [this file] ). 
Consistent with machine learning modelling, proteomics-based clustering outperformed transcriptomic clustering in distinguishing patient subtypes (Fig. 3a [rid=Fig3] , Supplementary Fig. 6a–h [this file] ). 
To further characterize the functional difference of each proteomic subtype, we conducted Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) using the subtype-specifically expressed proteins to identify subtype-specific activation or inhibition of specific pathways (Fig. 3d [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Fig. 7a–d [this file] ). By comparing these proteomic subtypes with previously established ALS subtypes of ALS-Ox, ALS-Glia, and ALS-TE , we found that ProS1 was mainly enriched in ALS-Glia subtype, ProS2 enriched in ALS-Ox subtype, and Pro S3 and S4 split into all the 3 subtypes with a slight enrichment in ALS-TE subtypes (Supplementary Fig. 7e [this file] ). We also employed an additional clustering methodology to classify AALS dataset (Supplementary Fig. 7f [this file] ). 
Next, we explored the protein modules across subtypes using Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA), identifying 14 proteomics-based co-expression modules (Fig. 3e [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Fig. 8a, b [this file] ). 
We examined the expression pattern of the PMA110 signature across the AALS proteomics subgroups and observed that certain proteins showed differential expression patterns among the subtypes (Supplementary Fig. 9a [this file] ). Differential expression analysis between each subtype and the control group in AALS dataset yielded a set of differentially expressed proteins, in contrast to the whole cohort analysis, indicating that the patient heterogeneity was indeed resolved at the molecular subtype level (Fig. 4b [rid=Fig4] , Supplementary Fig. 9b–e [this file] and Supplementary Data 2 [rid=MOESM3] ). Overlapping analysis of these subtype-specific DEPs with PMA110 yielded a list of 34 proteins (Fig. 4c [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Fig. 9f [this file] ). In contrast to the downregulation of RPS29 protein levels, RPS29 mRNA levels showed no reduction in ProS4 (Supplementary Fig. 9g [this file] ). However, no significant differences were detected in ProS4 and control group (Supplementary Fig. 9h [this file] ). 
We observed a significant reduction in protein translation rate after knockdown (Fig. 5a, b [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Fig. 10a [this file] ). In contrast, the frequency of translation initiation at near-cognate start codon was not affected by knockdown (Supplementary Fig. 10b, c [this file] ). 
To further understand the molecular mechanisms of loss in ALS, we performed Ribosome-seq (Ribo-seq) combined with RNA-seq to characterize the translatome and transcriptome in wildtype and knockdown cells and explore the RPS29-regulated cellular process (Supplementary Fig. 10d–g [this file] ). In line with the role of RPS29 in cytoplasmic ribosomes, protein translation pathway was downregulated at the protein translation level (Supplementary Fig. 10h [this file] ). 
We then confirmed a significant reduction in these proteins’ levels using western blotting and qRT-PCR (Fig. 6d, e [rid=Fig6] , Supplementary Fig. 10i [this file] ). 
Next, we explored the functional relevance of RPS29 in human iPSC differentiation-derived motor neurons (Supplementary Fig. 11a [this file] ). Compared to the RNA levels (Supplementary Fig. 11b [this file] ), immunofluorescence assays demonstrated decreased axon STMN2 levels after suppression, which was in line with the role of STMN2 in axon protection (Fig. 6j [rid=Fig6] ).

Coffee and green tea consumption were explored analogously to the other caffeinated beverages; however, we did not observe an association with motor severity over time in patients with iPD or -PD (Supplementary Tables 1 [this file] , 2 [this file] ). 
On the other hand, black tea has a more balanced prevalence among men and women or even a higher prevalence among women (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). 
When adjusting for sex, the linear mixed effects model confirmed the significant association between pesticide exposure and motor severity in PPMI-Online (β = 0.19, = 0.04, = 1.24 × 10 , adjusted α = 0.017, Supplementary Table 3A [this file] ), and there still was a trend in the same direction when assessing iPD patients from Fox Insight (β = 0.08, = 0.06, = 0.146). 
Secondly, we detected an association between smoking and motor aspects across time in patients with iPD in PPMI-Online, which remained unchanged after adjusting for sex (β = 0.12, = 0.04, = 3.17 × 10 , Supplementary Table 3B [this file] ). 
Thirdly, we detected an association between black tea consumption and less severe motor aspects across time in patients with -PD, specifically, which also remained unchanged after adjusting for sex (β = −0.53, = 0.23, = 0.028, Supplementary Table 3C [this file] ). 
The association with iPD remained after adjusting for sex in PPMI-Online (β = 0.13, = 0.03, = 2.60 × 10 , Supplementary Table 3D [this file] ) but got weaker in Fox Insight (iPD: β = 0.07, SE = 0.04, = 0.119, -PD: β = 0.35, = 0.22, = 0.111). 
Interestingly, we could confirm the association between black tea consumption and less severe motor aspects in patients with -PD (β = −0.41, = 0.18, = 0.026) (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] , Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). 
Unfortunately, the sample size of patients with PD and T2DM in our study cohorts was too small to explore the joint effects of T2DM and different lifestyle factors (Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). Interestingly, we did not observe an association with motor aspect severity over time (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). Furthermore, there is no correlation between the two beverages, as a substantial fraction of participants consumed both beverages, only one or none (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). 
Lastly, we observed that male iPD patients had more severe motor symptoms over time (Supplementary Table 3A–D [this file] ). 
The 35 month enrollment study time of the PPMI-Online cohort was divided into six to nine-month-long time periods, depending on the number of observations per time period (Supplementary Fig. 5A [this file] ). The 60-month enrollment study time of the Fox Insight cohort was divided into 10-month-long time periods (Supplementary Fig. 5B, C [this file] ). 
The model’s outcome was the log-transformed cumulative MDS-UPDRS Part II score (range 0–52) to achieve a more appropriate normal distribution of the outcome variable (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). The continuous fixed effect covariates (i.e., AAO & disease duration) were transformed using fractional polynomials to achieve a more linear correlation with the outcome variable (Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ).

Our study sample consists of 35,959 American patients with PD (Supplementary Table S1 [this file] ) from the Fox Insight study (Supplementary Text and Supplementary Figure S1 [this file] ). Most of the patients were of white/Caucasian ethnicity (89.9%) (Supplementary Table S1 [this file] ). 
Each questionnaire and specific variables within are described in detail in the Supplementary Text and Supplementary Table S2 [this file] . 
We first explored the association of coffee drinking before AAO with self-reported motor and non-motor features (Supplementary Table S2 [this file] ). When coffee drinking was used as a binary yes–no indication in a regression model with covariates AAE, gender, and disease duration (Table 1 [rid=Tab1] , Supplementary Table S3 [this file] ) coffee drinkers had fewer problems with chewing and swallowing (p = 0.0497, β = − 0.1435, SE = 0.0731). 
Furthermore, coffee did not show an association with the available non-motor symptoms (p > 0.05) (Table 2 [rid=Tab2] , Supplementary Table S4 [this file] ). When cups of coffee per week were used as a continuous variable, coffee drinking dosage showed a direct correlation with unexplained pains (p = 0.0168, β = 0.0083, SE = 0.0035) (Table 2 [rid=Tab2] , Supplementary Table S5 [this file] ). 
We further explored the association of aspirin intake before AAO with self-reported motor features (Supplementary Table S2 [this file] ). Aspirin intake (binary yes–no indication) showed a direct association with tremor (p = 0.0026, β = 0.3174, SE = 0.1054), chewing and swallowing problems (p = 0.0358, β = 0.1837, SE = 0.0875), and getting up (p = 0.0185, β = 0.2170, SE = 0.0922) (Table 1 [rid=Tab1] , Supplementary Table S3 [this file] ), indicating a higher probability to have tremor or problems with swallowing or getting out of a bed or a chair in the group of aspirin users compared to non-users. The exploratory association of aspirin intake with most motor symptoms was still robust after including the comorbidities (Supplementary Table S6 [this file] ) with the exception of chewing and swallowing: the association diminished when heart diseases (p = 0.1120, β = 0.1425, SE = 0.0897), arthritis (p = 0.0556, β = 0.1684, SE = 0.0880), back pain (p = 0.0591, β = 0.1661, SE = 0.0880), and surgeries with anesthesia (p = 0.0591, β = 0.1661, SE = 0.0880) were included (Supplementary Table S7 [this file] ). In addition, the association between aspirin intake and getting up diminished when heart diseases were included in the model (p = 0.0534, β = 0.1819, SE = 0.0941) (Supplementary Table S7 [this file] ). 
When assessing dosage effects, more aspirin taken per week associated with more problems with tremor (p = 0.0138, β = 0.0287, SE = 0.0117), chewing and swallowing (p = 0.0182, β = 0.0201, SE = 0.0085), walking and balance (p = 0.0106, β = 0.0253, SE = 0.0099), and getting up (p = 0.0182, β = 0.0231, SE = 0.0098) (Table 1 [rid=Tab1] , Supplementary Table S3 [this file] ). When potential confounding comorbidities were investigated, the association between the aspirin intake dosage and getting up diminished when back pain was included in the model (p = 0.0509, β = 0.0196, SE = 0.0100) (Supplementary Tables S6 [this file] , S7 [this file] ). 
In addition, we explored the association between aspirin intake status and non-motor symptoms (Table 2 [rid=Tab2] , Supplementary Tables S2 [this file] , S4). Aspirin intake (binary yes–no indication) exhibited a direct association with constipation (p = 0.0124, β = 0.2077, SE = 0.0831), unexplained pains (p = 0.0227, β = 0.1961, SE = 0.0861), problems remembering (p = 1 × 10 , β = 0.3662, SE = 0.0830), changed interest in sex (p = 0.0221, β = 0.2023, SE = 0.0884), and light-headedness (p = 0.0043, β = 0.2380, SE = 0.0833) (Table 2 [rid=Tab2] , Supplementary Table S5 [this file] ). When more aspirin pills per week were taken, more problems with non-motor symptoms such as constipation (p = 0.0037, β = 0.0251, SE = 0.0086), unexplained pains (p = 0.0320, β = 0.0178, SE = 0.0083), problems remembering (p = 0.0005, β = 0.0295, SE = 0.0085), feeling sad (p = 0.0344, β = 0.0177, SE = 0.0083), changed interest in sex (p = 0.0278, β = 0.0184, SE = 0.0084), and light-headedness (p = 0.0060, β = 0.0226, SE = 0.0082) (Table 2 [rid=Tab2] , Supplementary Table S5 [this file] ) were reported. The association between aspirin intake dosage and unexplained pains diminished when arthritis (p = 0.0672, β = 0.0154, SE = 0.0084) and back pain (p = 0.0896, β = 0.0142, SE = 0.0084) were included (Supplementary Tables S8 [this file] , S9 [this file] ). In addition, the association between aspirin intake dosage and feeling sad diminished when including heart diseases (p = 0.0806, β = 0.0147, SE = 0.0084), arthritis (p = 0.0513, β = 0.0164, SE = 0.0084), and back pain (p = 0.0527, β = 0.0163, SE = 0.0084) (Supplementary Tables S8 [this file] , S9 [this file] ). 
Lastly, we explored the association of smoking before AAO with self-reported motor features (Supplementary Table S2 [this file] ). Smoking directly correlated with excessive saliva and drooling (p = 0.0106, β = 0.1484, SE = 0.0580), chewing and swallowing problems (p = 0.0002, β = 0.2243, SE = 0.0603), and freezing (p = 0.0212, β = 0.1490, SE = 0.0646), when smoking was used as a binary yes–no indication (Table 1 [rid=Tab1] , Supplementary Table S3 [this file] ), indicating that smokers had more problems with too much saliva, problems with swallowing, and freezing. In addition, smoking dosage correlated with more problems with speech (p = 0.0062, β = 0.0089, SE = 0.0033), saliva excess and drooling (p = 0.0022, β = 0.0096, SE = 0.0031), chewing and swallowing (p < 1 × 10 , β = 0.0174, SE = 0.0031), walking and balance (p = 0.0038, β = 0.0101, SE = 0.0035), freezing (p = 0.0052, β = 0.0094, SE = 0.0034), and getting up (p = 0.0061, β = 0.0098, SE = 0.0036) (Table 1 [rid=Tab1] , Supplementary Table S3 [this file] ). Smoking duration also correlated with more problems with speech (p = 0.0454, β = 0.0119, SE = 0.0059), walking and balance (p = 4 × 10 , β = 0.0268, SE = 0.0065), freezing (p < 1 × 10 , β = 0.0277, SE = 0.0062), and getting up (p < 1 × 10 , β = 0.0366, SE = 0.0070) (Table 1 [rid=Tab1] , Supplementary Table S3 [this file] ). However, when investigating potential comorbidities, the association between smoking duration and speech diminished when heart diseases (p = 0.0526, β = 0.0115, SE = 0.0059) and lung diseases (p = 0.0591, β = 0.0113, SE = 0.0060) were included in the models, although heart diseases (p = 0.7074, β = 0.0752, SE = 0.2002) and lung diseases (p = 0.5828, β = 0.1105, SE = 0.2011) showed no association with speech either (Supplementary Tables S7 [this file] , S10 [this file] ). 
Most strikingly, smoking was directly associated with non-motor symptoms (Table 2 [rid=Tab2] , Supplementary Tables S2 [this file] , S4 [this file] ). Smokers experienced more unexplained pains (p < 1 × 10 , β = 0.2732, SE = 0.0595), problems remembering (p = 0.0001, β = 0.2176, SE = 0.0570), feeling sad (p < 1 × 10 , β = 0.3279, SE = 0.0579), anxiety (p < 1 × 10 , β = 0.3007, SE = 0.0604), changed interest in sex (p = 0.0013, β = 0.1959, SE = 0.0610), and light-headedness (p = 0.0005, β = 0.2000, SE = 0.0574) (Table 2 [rid=Tab2] , Supplementary Table S5 [this file] ). Smoking dosage correlated with more unexplained pains (p = 0.0003, β = 0.0114, SE = 0.0031), problems remembering (p = 6 × 10 , β = 0.0123, SE = 0.0030), feeling sad (p < 1 × 10 , β = 0.0152, SE = 0.0031), anxiety (p < 1 × 10 , β = 0.0161, SE = 0.0031), and light-headedness (p = 0.0001, β = 0.0117, SE = 0.0030) (Table 2 [rid=Tab2] , Supplementary Table S5 [this file] ). Smoking duration also correlated with more unexplained pains (p = 0.0134, β = 0.0140, SE = 0.0057), problems remembering (p = 0.0017, β = 0.0176, SE = 0.0056), feeling sad (p = 0.0470, β = 0.0112, SE = 0.0056), and changed interest in sex (p = 0.0372, β = 0.0123, SE = 0.0059) (Table 2 [rid=Tab2] , Supplementary Table S5 [this file] ). In addition, the association with a changed interest in sex (p = 0.0574, β = 0.0113, SE = 0.0059) diminished when heart diseases were included, although heart diseases itself showed no association with a changed interest in sex either (p = 0.0795, β = 0.3482, SE = 0.1986) (Supplementary Tables S9 [this file] , S11 [this file] ). 
As the most prominent association for smoking with non-motor symptoms, we additionally explored symptoms specifically related to mood (Supplementary Table S2 [this file] ). These include: dropped many activities and interests, life feels empty, getting bored often, being afraid something bad could happen, feeling helpless often, prefer staying at home, feeling to have more memory problems than other people, feeling pretty worthless, and feeling that situation is hopeless (p < 0.0025, β > 0.1955) (Table 3 [rid=Tab3] , Supplementary Tables S12 [this file] , S13 [this file] ). Smoking duration also showed the same direction for depression (p = 0.0422, β = 0.0123, SE = 0.0061), and factors associated with depression (p < 0.0039, β > 0.0178) (Table 3 [rid=Tab3] , Supplementary Table S13 [this file] ). When potential confounding comorbidities were investigated, all symptoms related to mood remained associated with smoking with the exception of depression: the association between smoking duration and depression diminished when heart diseases (p = 0.0544, β = 0.0117, SE = 0.0061) and lung diseases (p = 0.0584, β = 0.0116, SE = 0.0061) were included, although heart diseases (p = 0.1015, β = 0.3338, SE = 0.2038) and lung diseases (p = 0.3638, β = 0.1839, SE = 0.2025) showed no association with smoking duration either (Supplementary Tables S14 [this file] , S15 [this file] ). 
Since smokers in this cohort were on average older than non-smokers but had a shorter disease duration (Supplementary Figures S2 [this file] – S8 [this file] ), we would rather have expected less severe motor symptoms. 
When comparing the educational level in the different subgroups of lifestyle factors, we found smokers to have an overall lower educational level compared to non-smokers (Supplementary Figure S9 [this file] ). In contrast, there was a trend of a longer coffee drinking duration in the group of coffee drinkers with a higher educational level compared to coffee drinkers with a lower educational level (Supplementary Figure S10 [this file] ). There was no difference in the educational level between aspirin users and non-aspirin users (Supplementary Figure S11 [this file] ).

Using cognitively normal BLSA participants with concurrent 3‐T MRI and proteomic data (SomaScan; 7268 plasma proteins; Figure S1 [rid=alz14142-supitem-0002] ; Tables S1 [this file] and S2 [this file] ), we asked if machine learning measures of age‐ and AD‐related brain volume atrophy were associated with individual plasma proteins (FDR < 0.05) and broader proteomic signatures (uncorrected < 0.05). 
In linear regression models adjusted for demographic, physiological, and comorbid variables, five proteins were associated with brain atrophy after correction for multiple comparisons (FDR < 0.05), including a NPTX2 and a TNF‐receptor (TNFRSF10D) associated with lower subcortical atrophy patterns (R1), a chemokine (CXCL12) associated with greater parieto‐temporal lobe atrophy (R3), and an extracellular matrix glycoprotein (EFEMP1) and a glycolytic enzyme (ALDOC) that were associated with higher and lower AD‐related atrophy (SPARE‐AD), respectively (Figure 2B [rid=alz14142-fig-0002] and Table S3 [this file] ). For instance, the AD‐related atrophy associated with EFEMP1 (standardized = 0.164, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.100, 0.229, FDR = 0.005) was more robust than the AD‐related atrophy associated with NfL (standardized = 0.124, 95% CI: 0.052, 0.196, < 0.001), GFAP (standardized = 0.101, 95% CI: 0.035, 0.167, = 0.003), and age (standardized = 0.029, 95% CI: 0.0244, 0.0342, < 0.001) (Table S3 [this file] ). As expected, VBM analyses conducted in this same set of participants showed NPTX2 and TNFRSF10D were most strongly related to subcortical brain volumes (e.g., basal ganglia), CXCL12 displayed robust associations with parieto‐temporal volumes (e.g., temporal gyrus), and EFEMP1 and ALDOC were associated with volumes in AD‐sensitive brain regions (e.g., hippocampus) (Figure 2C [rid=alz14142-fig-0002] ; Figure S3 [rid=alz14142-supitem-0002] ; Table S4 [this file] ). 
The broader proteomic signatures (uncorrected < 0.05) of each brain atrophy measure were enriched for distinct biological processes as well as specific cell and tissue types (Figure 2D [rid=alz14142-fig-0002] ; Figure 3A–F [rid=alz14142-fig-0003] ; Tables S5–S7 [this file] ). The proteomic signatures of all brain atrophy measures were enriched for brain‐ and immune‐specific proteins (Table S8 [this file] ), in line with prior evidence suggesting that circulating inflammatory proteins can influence the structural integrity of brain regions that are vulnerable in aging and neurodegenerative conditions.[rid=alz14142-bib-0015] ,[rid=alz14142-bib-0043] These results suggest that different brain atrophy patterns are associated with distinct proteo‐biological profiles, and that a subset of five plasma proteins may be especially important molecular drivers of age‐ and AD‐related neurodegeneration. 
We also leveraged MRI and Olink proteomics data from the UKB ( = 3150; age = 63.7[SD = 7.8]; 51.6% female; Figure S4 [rid=alz14142-supitem-0002] ; Table S9 [this file] ) as part of a cross‐platform, external validation of protein‐brain atrophy associations. Of the five plasma proteins related to brain atrophy patterns in the BLSA using SomaScan, two (EFEMP1, CXCL12) were quantified in the UKB and showed strong correlations (i.e., > 0.5) across the SomaScan and Olink platforms, as evidenced by previously published results in the deCODE study[rid=alz14142-bib-0027] ( = 1514; Table S10 [this file] ). We replicated EFEMP1's association with greater AD‐related atrophy (standardized = 0.120, 95% CI: 0.024, 0.216, = 0.014), and although we did not replicate CXCL12's association with parieto‐temporal lobe atrophy (standardized = −0.007, 95% CI: −0.079, 0.065, = 0.845), we found it was associated with higher perisylvian (R5) atrophy (standardized = 0.094, 95% CI: 0.027, 0.161, = 0.006; Table S11 [this file] ). 
Analyses of Aβ , GFAP, and NfL included 1017 BLSA participants, and pTau‐181 analyses included 690 BLSA participants, all of whom were cognitively normal (Figure S5 [rid=alz14142-supitem-0002] ; Table S1 [this file] ). EFEMP1 and CXCL12, (i.e., plasma proteins associated with higher levels of parieto‐temporal and AD‐specific brain atrophy, respectively), were associated with elevated pTau‐181; while EFEMP1 showed additional associations with elevated GFAP and NfL, CXCL12's positive associations with GFAP ( = 0.085) and NfL ( = 0.051) were not statistically significant (Figure 4A,B [rid=alz14142-fig-0004] ; Table S12 [this file] ). 
We also examined if brain atrophy‐related plasma proteins were associated with cognitive status using BLSA participants who were otherwise excluded from preceding analyses ( = 113; MCI = 50, Dementia = 63) (Figure S6 [rid=alz14142-supitem-0002] ; Table S1 [this file] ). Consistent with their pathogenic effects on parieto‐temporal and AD‐related brain atrophy, respectively, EFEMP1 and CXCL12 were related to higher risk of cognitive impairment (Figure 4B [rid=alz14142-fig-0004] ; Table S13 [this file] ). 
Using data from the Emory Goizueta (ADRC; = 36; Table S14 [this file] ),[rid=alz14142-bib-0028] we investigated if proteins associated with brain atrophy in the BLSA were related to CSF biomarkers, cognitive performance, and AD risk in this cohort. Consistent with the association between EFEMP1 and greater AD‐specific brain atrophy observed in the BLSA, EFEMP1 was related to higher CSF pTau‐181 (Figure 4C [rid=alz14142-fig-0004] , Table S15 [this file] ). 
Consistent with its deleterious associations observed in preceding analyses, higher EFEMP1 was associated with lower performance in processing speed, non‐verbal reasoning, vocabulary, and general cognitive functioning (Figure 4E [rid=alz14142-fig-0004] ; Table S16 [this file] ). Examination of neuroimaging measures showed CXCL12 was related to higher fractional anisotropy, reflecting preserved white matter microstructure (Figure 4F [rid=alz14142-fig-0004] ; Table S16 [this file] ). 
We also examined if plasma proteins associated with brain atrophy in the BLSA were associated with 20‐ and 8‐year incident dementia risk in the ARIC study using plasma that was collected in mid‐life ( = 11,596; age = 57.1[SD = 5.7]) and late‐life ( = 4288; age = 75.2[SD = 5.0]), respectively (Figure S7 [rid=alz14142-supitem-0002] ; Table S17 [this file] ). Plasma proteins linked to greater brain atrophy in the BLSA, namely EFEMP1 (HR = 2.01, 95% CI: 1.50, 2.72) and CXCL12 (HR = 1.42, 95% CI: 1.10, 1.83), were associated with greater 8‐year dementia risk when measured in late‐life, while CXCL12 (HR = 1.28, 95% CI: 1.05, 1.57) was also associated with greater 20‐year dementia risk when measured in mid‐life (Figure 4G [rid=alz14142-fig-0004] ; Table S18 [this file] ). 
Using curated GWAS summary statistics and pQTLs identified by the deCODE study ( = 35,559),[rid=alz14142-bib-0033] we found EFEMP1 variants that influenced its protein levels in plasma as well as differences in cortical thickness, cortical surface area, and cognitive functioning (Figure 5A [rid=alz14142-fig-0005] ; Table S19 [this file] ). We also identified CXCL12 variants that influenced its protein levels in plasma as well as differences in cortical thickness, temporal gyrus thickness, cortical surface area, and sulcal depth (Figure 5A [rid=alz14142-fig-0005] ; Table S19 [this file] ). 
We then used the BLSA to validate EFEMP1 and CXCL12 pQTLs identified by the deCODE study, and to examine whether these variants were associated with AD‐related atrophy (SPARE‐AD) and parieto‐temporal atrophy (R3), respectively.[rid=alz14142-bib-0044] Using and pQTLs, we replicated SNP associations with plasma protein levels for both EFEMP1 and CXCL12 ( = 718; Figure S9 [rid=alz14142-supitem-0002] ; Tables S1, S20, S21 [this file] ). 
EFEMP1 and CXCL12 were not causally implicated in SPARE‐AD and hippocampal volume differences, respectively (Figures S12, S13 [rid=alz14142-supitem-0002] ; Tables S22, S23 [this file] ). 
Leveraging SomaScan plasma and CSF protein measurements from the Johns Hopkins Hospital Neurology Clinic ( = 194; Figure S14 [rid=alz14142-supitem-0002] ; Table S24 [this file] ), we found CXCL12 (rho = 0.21, = 0.003) was weakly correlated across biofluids, while EFEMP1 showed a marginal positive correlation (rho = 0.12, = 0.097). CXCL12 showed a similar correlation (rho = 0.31, = 0.063) across biofluids in an independent cohort (Emory Goizueta ADRC; = 36; Figure S15 [rid=alz14142-supitem-0002] ; Table S25 [this file] ). 
We confirmed existing studies have externally validated all plasma protein measurements (SOMAmer reagents) using one or more biochemical techniques (e.g., mass spectroscopy, proximity extension assay, etc.) (Table S26 [this file] ). We found EFEMP1 is highly expressed in genitourinary cell types as well as astrocytes, and is enriched in arteries at tissue‐wide expression levels, while CXCL12 is highly expressed in fibroblasts, adipocytes, and tissue‐resident macrophages (Kupffer cells in liver tissue), but not enriched for a specific tissue type (Figure 6A [rid=alz14142-fig-0006] ; Tables S27, S28 [this file] ). All cognate genes encoding plasma proteins were differentially expressed in AD (versus control) brain tissue, especially in the parahippocampal gyrus, where CXCL12 and EFEMP1 tended to be upregulated (Figure S16 [rid=alz14142-supitem-0002] ; Table S29 [this file] ). In neurovascular tissue, all cognate genes with available RNA‐seq data showed differential expression in AD versus control brains across multiple blood‐brain barrier cell types, particularly arterial and capillary endothelial cells (Figure S17 [rid=alz14142-supitem-0002] ; Table S30 [this file] ). After identifying molecules downstream of CXCL12 and EFEMP1, we found this network was enriched for granulocyte adhesion and transcriptional activation, suggesting these proteins may exert their effects by modulating immune cell migration and homeostatic gene regulation (Figure 6B [rid=alz14142-fig-0006] ; Table S31 [this file] ).

Using data from the BLSA along with the SomaScan v4.1 Inflammation and Immune Response Panel, we examined how the baseline levels of 942 immune-related proteins in plasma related to subsequent rates of change in cortical Aβ levels ( Figure 1 [rid=F1] ; sTable 1 [rid=SD2] – 3 [rid=SD2] ; sFigure 1 [this file] ). 
Rates of change in cortical Aβ were elevated for Aβ+ (n=44) compared to Aβ− (n=94) participants ( Figure 2A [rid=F2] ; sFigure 2 [this file] ), which equated to an additional increase of 4.38 centiloids/year. 
While QQ plots (i.e., observed p values compared to expected p values from a theoretical χ2 distribution) did not suggest inflated Type-I error (λ=0.68; sFigure 4A [this file] ), permutation testing (100 rounds with Aβ slopes randomly shuffled across participants) did highlight the potential for the identification of false positives. These conflicting patterns may be attributed to the inherently interrelated structure of the immune proteome (i.e., observations are not truly independent) or other unknown sources of bias ( sFigure 4B [this file] ). 
Plasma levels of one candidate protein (APOE2) were associated with greater Aβ accumulation across Aβ+ participants, Aβ− participants, and the whole sample, whereas another candidate protein (CAT) was associated with different effects on Aβ progression depending on whether participants were Aβ+ or Aβ− ( Figure 2E [rid=F2] ; sFigure 3A [this file] – D [this file] ). Proteins associated with more rapid Aβ accumulation among Aβ+ participants tended to be associated with attenuated Aβ accumulation among Aβ− participants ( sFigure 3C [this file] ). 
For the twelve candidate proteins whose baseline levels and rates of change were related to altered Aβ accumulation in BLSA, we utilized data collected in the ARIC study (n=272; age=75.7 [SD=5.2]; 56.2% female; 59.6% white; sTable 10 [rid=SD2] ; sFigure 5 [this file] ) to determine if preceding rates of change in these protein levels might be associated with subsequent Aβ status. Of the candidate proteins measured in ARIC, greater increases in one (CAT) over mid- to late-life were related to increased odds of Aβ+ ( sFigure 6 [this file] ; sTable 11 [rid=SD2] ). 
Among BLSA participants with available genotyping data, we replicated associations for 13 of the 21 candidate proteins with available pQTLs (i.e., at least one SNP per protein was associated with protein abundance in plasma; sTable 3 [rid=SD2] , 12 [rid=SD2] ; sFigure 7 [this file] ). 
We then asked how candidate proteins related to cross-sectional tau-PET levels in the BLSA (n=78; sTable 3 [rid=SD2] ; sFigure 8 [this file] ). Similar patterns were found in minimally adjusted, stratified analyses (Aβ+ n=20; Aβ− n=58), where we also noted CAT’s association with greater tau-PET levels in the ITG among Aβ+ participants ( sFigure 11A [this file] ). 
We also examined whether candidate proteins were related to longitudinal changes in plasma ADRD biomarkers in the BLSA (n=638 for Aβ ratio, NfL, GFAP; n=541 for pTau-181) measured over a median follow-up time of 5.1 years (IQR: 4.0, 7.1) for Aβ , GFAP and NfL analyses and 5.0 years (IQR: 4.0, 7.0) for pTau181 analyses ( sTable 3 [rid=SD2] , sFigure 9 [this file] , 10 [this file] ). Given that ADRD biomarker trajectories may be influenced by the degree of underlying AD pathology, these analyses adjusted for Aβ status among participants without Aβ PET using plasma Aβ status (defined by plasma Aβ because it was available in a larger set of participants and illustrated comparable performance for discriminating Aβ PET status relative to other biomarkers; sFigure 11B [this file] – C [this file] ). Of the proteins associated with lower rates of cortical Aβ progression, one was related to greater increases in GFAP (KITLG), one was associated with lower increases in pTau-181 (CSF3), and another was related to lower increases in NfL (SMS), especially among Aβ+ participants ( sFigure 11D [this file] ). 
To determine if plasma proteins associated with cortical amyloid accumulation might also influence dementia risk, we utilized data collected in the ARIC study to examine the associations of candidate proteins measured in mid-life (n=11,596; age=57.1 [SD=5.7]; 55.7% female; 77.0% white) and late-life (n=4,288; age=75.2 [SD=5.0]; 57.9% female; 81.8% white) with 20- and 8-year dementia risk, respectively ( sTable 10 [rid=SD2] ; sFigure 12 [this file] ). 
Five cognate genes ( ) were highly expressed in at least one CNS cell type, and another ten were undetectable in CNS cells; among all 76 cell types, cognate genes were most frequently enriched in myeloid cells, including Kupffer cells, dendritic cells, macrophages, and monocytes ( sTable 19 [rid=SD2] , 20 [rid=SD2] ; sFigure 13 [this file] ). 
Single cell RNA-seq showed 18 (75%) cognate genes were differentially expressed in one or more prominent CNS cell types in AD; here, differential expression was most evident in neurons and astrocytes, and these patterns were more robust with more advanced AD pathology ( sTable 22 [rid=SD2] ; sFigure 14A [this file] – C [this file] ). Among neurovascular cell types, 21 (81%) cognate genes were differentially expressed in AD, where patterns of AD-related expression were most apparent in hippocampal astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, vascular smooth muscle cells and meningeal fibroblasts ( sTable 23 [rid=SD2] ); candidate proteins with potential mechanistic links to Aβ progression showed altered expression most prominently in ependymal cells (CD36), arterial endothelial cells (KRT19), and cortical astrocytes (CAT) ( sFigure 14D [this file] ). 
Pathway analyses showed candidate proteins were most strongly enriched for atherogenic, retinoic acid and macrophage-specific reactive oxygen species (ROS) signaling cascades ( Figure 4B [rid=F4] ; sTable 28 [rid=SD2] ; sFigure 15 [this file] – 17 [this file] ), which have been previously implicated in AD . 
Alternatively, these results could suggest that upregulated CAT expression is an adaptive process triggered by early brain amyloidosis which is blunted among carriers of CAT’s rs1001179 T allele, and ultimately limits further accumulation of Aβ pathology in the context of high Aβ burden, a disease stage otherwise associated with greater tau burden and dementia risk ( sFigure 18 [this file] ). 
Aβ was used to define Aβ status rather than pTau-181 or Aβ /pTau-181 so that such cut-points could be applicable to the larger set of participants with concurrent SomaScan measurements (i.e., n=l,015 with N4PE measurements versus n=688 with V2 measurements) and because its optimal cut point illustrated comparatively similar performance in discriminating Aβ PET status ( sFigure 11B [this file] – C [this file] ).

Notably, the 32 candidate proteins’ p values obtained from permutation testing were rarely (if at all) lower than their observed p values in our primary analyses, suggesting that many of the detected associations are not due to random chance ( sTable 5 [this file] ). 
Notably, only one of the 32 candidate proteins (CD36) was associated with Aβ status (+/−) at baseline, suggesting limited overlap between the peripheral immune proteins associated with rates of Aβ accumulation and those associated with elevated Aβ ( Figure 2C [rid=F2] ; sTable 6 [this file] ). In addition to steeper rates of Aβ progression and increased odds of Aβ+, higher CD36 was linked to a younger estimated age of Aβ+ onset ( Figure 2D [rid=F2] ; sTable 7 [this file] ). With few exceptions (e.g., CDCP1, CCL2), results were consistent in models adjusted for physiological and comorbid variables only ( sTable 4 [this file] ). In sensitivity analyses adjusting for sample storage time, effect estimates remained largely similar, with the exception of APOE2, COL5A1, KITLG, SH2D1A, SMS, which showed effect size decrements >10% ( sTable 4 [this file] ). Candidate protein associations did not show effect modification by sex, suggesting their relationships with Aβ accumulation did not statistically differ between men and women ( sTable 4 [this file] ). 
Consistent with the effects of baseline protein levels, greater increases in two proteins (S100A8, NCF1) and greater reductions in another two (KRT19, APOC3) were associated with blunted Aβ accumulation among Aβ+ participants, while greater reductions in another two (LTA, CSF3) were associated with higher rates of Aβ accumulation ( Figure 2F [rid=F2] – G [rid=F2] ; sTable 8 [this file] – 9 [this file] ). 
For the twelve candidate proteins whose baseline levels and rates of change were related to altered Aβ accumulation in BLSA, we utilized data collected in the ARIC study (n=272; age=75.7 [SD=5.2]; 56.2% female; 59.6% white; sTable 10 [this file] ; sFigure 5 [rid=SD1] ) to determine if preceding rates of change in these protein levels might be associated with subsequent Aβ status. Of the candidate proteins measured in ARIC, greater increases in one (CAT) over mid- to late-life were related to increased odds of Aβ+ ( sFigure 6 [rid=SD1] ; sTable 11 [this file] ). 
Among BLSA participants with available genotyping data, we replicated associations for 13 of the 21 candidate proteins with available pQTLs (i.e., at least one SNP per protein was associated with protein abundance in plasma; sTable 3 [this file] , 12 [this file] ; sFigure 7 [rid=SD1] ). 
To formally test if genetic variation that influences CAT, CD36, and KRT19 protein levels in plasma may be causally related to brain amyloidosis, we combined their pQTLs with summary statistics from a GWAS of cortical Aβ PET levels (n=13,409) , and conducted two-sample MR ( Figure 3G [rid=F3] ; sTable 13 [this file] , 14 [this file] ). 
We then asked how candidate proteins related to cross-sectional tau-PET levels in the BLSA (n=78; sTable 3 [this file] ; sFigure 8 [rid=SD1] ). Several candidate proteins linked to more rapid cortical Aβ accumulation were associated with lower regional tau-PET levels at baseline, including CXCL12, TFIP2 and IRF4 (Braak I-II) as well as NPM1 (Braak III-IV) ( Figure 3H [rid=F3] ; sTable 15 [this file] ), suggesting that a subset of the candidate proteins may have a pleiotropic association with two hallmarks of AD. 
We also examined whether candidate proteins were related to longitudinal changes in plasma ADRD biomarkers in the BLSA (n=638 for Aβ ratio, NfL, GFAP; n=541 for pTau-181) measured over a median follow-up time of 5.1 years (IQR: 4.0, 7.1) for Aβ , GFAP and NfL analyses and 5.0 years (IQR: 4.0, 7.0) for pTau181 analyses ( sTable 3 [this file] , sFigure 9 [rid=SD1] , 10 [rid=SD1] ). Eight (25%) candidate proteins linked to greater cortical Aβ accumulation were associated with changes in ADRD biomarkers, including CXCL12 (higher increases in GFAP), C1Q (higher increases in NFL), and ETNK1 (greater decreases in Aβ , indicative of greater increases in brain Aβ), while two others (IL16, COL5A1) were related to attenuated increases in pTau-181 ( Figure 3I [rid=F3] ; sTable 16 [this file] ). 
To determine if plasma proteins associated with cortical amyloid accumulation might also influence dementia risk, we utilized data collected in the ARIC study to examine the associations of candidate proteins measured in mid-life (n=11,596; age=57.1 [SD=5.7]; 55.7% female; 77.0% white) and late-life (n=4,288; age=75.2 [SD=5.0]; 57.9% female; 81.8% white) with 20- and 8-year dementia risk, respectively ( sTable 10 [this file] ; sFigure 12 [rid=SD1] ). Surprisingly, higher plasma APOC3 levels, which were also linked to greater rates of Aβ accumulation in the BLSA, were associated with decreased dementia risk in ARIC when measured during late-life ( Figure 3J [rid=F3] ; sTable 17 [this file] ). 
Leveraging SomaScan plasma and CSF protein measurements from the Johns Hopkins Neurology Clinic (n=194), we found the levels of seven proteins (CCL2 [r=0.21], COL5A1 [r=0.22], CUL1 [r=0.15], KITLG [r=0.14], NCF1 [r=0.25], CXCL12 [r=0.19], TFRC [r=0.16]) were positively correlated across biofluids ( sTable 18 [this file] ). 
Five cognate genes ( ) were highly expressed in at least one CNS cell type, and another ten were undetectable in CNS cells; among all 76 cell types, cognate genes were most frequently enriched in myeloid cells, including Kupffer cells, dendritic cells, macrophages, and monocytes ( sTable 19 [this file] , 20 [this file] ; sFigure 13 [rid=SD1] ). 
Bulk RNA-seq results from comprehensive post-mortem tissue collections showed that every cognate gene with available expression data was differentially expressed at the RNA level in AD, with another three (CAT, APOE, NPM1) also differentially expressed at the protein level ( sTable 21 [this file] ). Single cell RNA-seq showed 18 (75%) cognate genes were differentially expressed in one or more prominent CNS cell types in AD; here, differential expression was most evident in neurons and astrocytes, and these patterns were more robust with more advanced AD pathology ( sTable 22 [this file] ; sFigure 14A [rid=SD1] – C [rid=SD1] ). Among neurovascular cell types, 21 (81%) cognate genes were differentially expressed in AD, where patterns of AD-related expression were most apparent in hippocampal astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, vascular smooth muscle cells and meningeal fibroblasts ( sTable 23 [this file] ); candidate proteins with potential mechanistic links to Aβ progression showed altered expression most prominently in ependymal cells (CD36), arterial endothelial cells (KRT19), and cortical astrocytes (CAT) ( sFigure 14D [rid=SD1] ). To determine if AD-related patterns of cognate gene expression were translatable to preclinical models, we leveraged published results which assessed protein and gene expression in brain tissue of AD transgenic mice and their wild type littermates ( sTable 24 [this file] ). 
Of the 24 genes detected in one or more microglia subtype, 21 (88%) were differentially regulated in at least one subtype ( Figure 4A [rid=F4] ; sTable 25 [this file] ). Cognate genes encoding candidate proteins linked to steeper amyloid accumulation in the BLSA tended to be upregulated in DAMs and IRMs, but downregulated among HMs. To confirm DAM enrichment among candidate proteins, we also assessed cognate gene expression in a murine microglia transcriptomes reported elsewhere ; of the 12 genes detected in this independent sample, 9 (75%) were differentially expressed in DAM, further suggesting a robust enrichment of Aβ-sensitive candidate proteins ( sTable 26 [this file] ). 
Existing studies externally validated 21 (66%) candidate protein measurements (SOMAmer reagents) using one or more biochemical techniques (e.g., mass spectrometry, proximity extension assay etc.,) ( sTable 27 [this file] ). Pathway analyses showed candidate proteins were most strongly enriched for atherogenic, retinoic acid and macrophage-specific reactive oxygen species (ROS) signaling cascades ( Figure 4B [rid=F4] ; sTable 28 [this file] ; sFigure 15 [rid=SD1] – 17 [rid=SD1] ), which have been previously implicated in AD . We also identified pro-inflammatory mediators (TNF, IL1-β, lipopolysaccharide (LPS)) as their strongest upstream regulators, consistent with prior studies showing pro-inflammatory mechanisms underlying neurodegeneration may be mediated through alterations in the plasma immune proteome ( Figure 4C [rid=F4] ; sTable 29 [this file] ). Further examination of their canonical functions revealed candidate proteins may influence rates of Aβ accumulation through a variety of complementary biological mechanisms, including recruiting peripheral immune cells, modulating proteostasis, and regulating BBB permeability ( sTable 30 [this file] ; Figure 5 [rid=F5] ). Protein interaction analyses revealed an extensive network among candidate proteins, including ample co-expression patterns ( Figure 4D [rid=F4] ; sTable 31 [this file] ). Lastly, we found 15 medications that target the levels of seven candidate proteins, suggesting that such drugs may have potential for repurposing in the treatment of AD, especially among individuals vulnerable to accelerated cortical Aβ accumulation ( Figure 4D [rid=F4] ; sTable 32 [this file] ). 
For a subset of participants without a blood sample available at baseline, a blood sample from the next closest preceding BLSA visit was used ( sTable 2 [this file] ); participants were excluded if the closest preceding visit with an available blood sample was >1 visit before baseline. 
Details of statistical analyses (e.g., predictor variables, response variables, covariates etc.,) are summarized in the supplementary materials [rid=SD1] ( sTable 33 [this file] ). 
Data generated in the current study are available in this article (and its supplementary figures [rid=SD1] or supplementary tables [this file] ), upon reasonable request, or in an online public repository.

Hoarding and depression symptom severity in HD and non-HD participants over time are depicted in Figures 1 [rid=F1] – 3 [rid=F3] (hoarding subscales in Supplemental Figures 1 [this file] – 3 [this file] ). While depression severity decreased over time in the UCSF sample ( Figure 1 [rid=F1] ), we observed no significant difference in depression severity among participants with and without HD at baseline or 30-month follow-up (Baseline: 19.1 (3.6) vs. 17.6 (2.0), t(25) = −1.84, p=0.08; 30 month: 11.1 (6.2) vs. 8.3 (5.6), t(65) = −1.75, p=0.09; Supplemental Table 1 [this file] ). In contrast, in the full online sample, depression severity was higher among participants with HD relative to those without at all timepoints, with mean total scores in both groups remaining relatively stable over time ( Figure 2 [rid=F2] and Supplemental Table 2 [this file] ). 
Bivariate Pearson correlation coefficients between SI-R total scores at 12, 24 and 30 months ranged between 0.73 and 0.91 ( Supplemental Figure 4 [this file] ). SI-R subscales were also strongly correlated across time ( Supplemental Figures 5 [this file] – 7 [this file] ). 
In the online sample, bivariate Pearson correlations between HRS total scores were also high, especially between consecutive timepoint pairs (all correlation coefficients between 0.75 and 0.83, Supplemental Figure 8 [this file] ). The magnitude of the correlations between HRS subscore measures across time were also moderate to large in size (all correlations between 0.55 and 0.76) ( Supplemental Figures 9 [this file] – 11 [this file] , only 0, 12, 24, and 30 months depicted). A similar pattern was observed among online participants with LLD, wherein correlation coefficients between HRS total scores ranged between 0.67 and 0.90 across timepoint pairs ( Supplemental Figures 12 [this file] – 15 [this file] , only 0, 12, 24, and 30 months depicted). 
However, there were no significant cross-lagged paths between hoarding and depression, indicating that higher than expected depression severity did not predict higher than expected hoarding severity six months later, and vice versa (Hoarding to Depression: unstandardized =0.01, z = 0.306, p=0.760; Depression to Hoarding: unstandardized =0.01, z = 0.192, p = 0.848; Supplemental Figure 16 [this file] ). 
For HAM-D total score, the two groups did not significantly differ from one another at either timepoint (test statistics and p-values provided in Supplemental Table 1 [this file] ). 
For both HRS-SR total score and PHQ-9 total score, the two groups significantly differed (p<0.05) from one another at all timepoints (test statistics and p-values provided in Supplemental Table 2 [this file] ). 
For PHQ-9 total score, the two groups significantly differed from one another (p<0.05) at 6 months and 12 months only (test statistics and p-values provided in Supplemental Table 2 [this file] ).

In the current study, we included 13,733 individuals from the GNPC cohort, with n = 8,372 non-impaired (NI) controls, 4,217 Alzheimer’s disease (AD), 175 frontotemporal dementia (FTD), 185 Parkinson’s disease dementia (PDD), 540 Parkinson’s disease (PD), and 244 amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cases ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). Most individuals with AD had cognitive impairment scores indicative of mild or moderate AD ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
To establish a robust analytical foundation, we began with Version 1 of the GNPC dataset, which comprises plasma proteomic profiles generated across 16 international contributing sites, totalling 13,733 individuals across five major neurodegenerative diseases: AD ( = 4,217; 13 sites), FTD ( = 175; 6 sites), PDD ( = 185; 10 sites), PD ( = 540; 8 sites), and ALS ( = 244; 1 site), alongside non-impaired (NI) controls ( = 8,372; 15 sites) ( Fig. 2a [rid=F2] ; Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ) . 
Using this framework, we identified = 2,524 AD, 580 PD, 101 FTD, 85 ALS, and 64 PDD high-confidence plasma protein associations relative to NI controls ( Supplementary Tables 2 [this file] – 6 [this file] ). Functional enrichment analyses revealed a mixture of shared and disease-specific biology ( Fig. 4a [rid=F4] – c [rid=F4] ; Supplementary Tables 7 [this file] – 9 [this file] ). A prominent core signature was shared between AD and PD, involving cell stress adaptation and immune-metabolic regulation, including negative regulation of apoptosis, glycolytic and gluconeogenic metabolism, viral response, protein phosphorylation, angiogenesis, blood coagulation, and cell adhesion ( Fig. 4a [rid=F4] ; Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). Despite this common axis, AD exhibited the broadest systemic molecular footprint, with additional enrichment in intracellular trafficking, membrane receptor signalling, and metabolic control ( Fig. 4a [rid=F4] ; Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). PD showed a more focused enrichment, dominated by ubiquitin-mediated proteostasis ( Fig. 4a [rid=F4] ; Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). AD and PD both demonstrated enrichment in kinase, receptor, and cytokine/chemokine binding activities, indicating shared disruption of phospho-signaling and inflammatory mediator networks ( Fig. 4b [rid=F4] ; Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). In contrast, PD-specific enrichment of ubiquitin-protein transferase activity highlights proteostatic failure as a core mechanistic feature of PD ( Fig. 4b [rid=F4] ; Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). AD was characterized by systemic pathway disruption, with broad enrichment across complement activation, phagocytic signalling, metabolic reprogramming, extracellular matrix remodelling, and second messenger signalling ( Fig. 4c [rid=F4] – h [rid=F4] ; Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). PD mirrored many of these pathways but uniquely retained ubiquitin-proteasome and T cell receptor signalling, further emphasizing proteostasis and adaptive immune signalling imbalance ( Fig. 4c [rid=F4] – g [rid=F4] ; Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). 
Biological processes enrichment was confined to muscle contraction ( Fig. 4a [rid=F4] ; Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ), and molecular functions were restricted to actin and calcium ion binding, consistent with changes in cytoskeletal integrity and excitation-contraction coupling ( Fig. 4b [rid=F4] ; Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). KEGG enrichment in cardiomyopathy-associated pathways further supported peripheral neuromuscular involvement ( Fig. 4h [rid=F4] ; Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). FTD showed limited but biologically relevant enrichment, overlapping with AD in p53 and JAK–STAT signalling and uniquely implicating transcriptional misregulation ( Fig. 4f [rid=F4] – g [rid=F4] ; Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). 
In PD, disease-associated proteins showed significant enrichment in lymphoid organs, including lymph nodes and bone marrow ( Fig. 5a [rid=F5] ; Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ). 
In contrast, AD plasma proteins demonstrated widespread and highly significant enrichment across multiple organ systems, including immune and lymphoid tissues (tonsil, lymph node, spleen, appendix, bone marrow), metabolic organs (liver, pancreas), reproductive tissues (ovary, endometrium, prostate, seminal vesicle, epididymis), and the urogenital tract (bladder) ( Fig. 5b [rid=F5] ; Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ). Cell type-specific analyses further revealed that ovary, bone marrow, and pancreas harboured the greatest diversity of enriched cellular populations ( Fig. 5c [rid=F5] ; Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ). Leading-edge gene set integration across enriched organs and cell types revealed three coherent biological modules ( Fig. 5d [rid=F5] ; Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ). 
High-centrality compounds were strongly enriched for redox cofactors and electron transport mediators (NADH, FAD, glutathione, pyridoxal phosphate), indicating disrupted redox homeostasis and mitochondrial bioenergetics as core AD-specific metabolic targets ( Fig. 5e [rid=F5] ; Supplementary Table 13 [this file] ). Central carbon metabolites (β-D-glucose, citric acid, ATP, L-glutamate, L-aspartate) further linked AD to altered glycolytic-TCA coupling and neurotransmitter-linked anaplerotic metabolism ( Fig. 5e [rid=F5] ; Supplementary Table 13 [this file] ). Compounds associated with post-translational modification and proteostasis control (GDP cycling, ADP-ribosylation intermediates, adenylate analogs) mapped to broad intracellular stress adaptation and protein-quality control systems ( Fig. 5e [rid=F5] ; Supplementary Table 13 [this file] ). 
The AD cohort was already age and sex balanced relative to NI controls; therefore, the AD high confidence protein set was retained in full under the matched analyses ( Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). These included components of lipoprotein metabolism (APOB), complement and inflammatory signalling (C3, GDF2), nucleotide and redox homeostasis (CTPS1, NT5C, GLRX3), and protein folding and translational control (CCT5, PA2G4, RRS12, ALAD, PGP), together indicating systemic metabolic-immune dysregulation as a core AD plasma signature ( Fig. 6 [rid=F6] ; Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). This is a regulator of heparan sulfate biosynthesis and extracellular signalling ( Fig. 6 [rid=F6] ; Supplementary Table 14 [this file] ), consistent with the limited systemic proteomic signal and greater clinico-pathological heterogeneity observed in FTD. No protein associations survived the matched analysis in PDD ( Supplementary Table 15 [this file] ), reflective of the underpowered nature of PDD cases. In PD, 12 proteins remained robust after matching ( Supplementary Table 16 [this file] ). These included proteins associated with sarcomere structure (MYOM2, MYBPC1, ACTN2, TNNI2), muscle regeneration and contractile machinery (KLHL41, PDLIM3, APOBEC2), and neuromuscular synaptic organization (LRTM1, ART3) ( Fig. 6 [rid=F6] ; Supplementary Table 17 [this file] ), consistent with peripheral neuromuscular involvement as a defining systemic feature of ALS. 
Summary results generated in this manuscript are available in Supplementary Tables (S2 [this file] – S6 [this file] and S14 [this file] – S17 [this file] ).
