The GNPC V1 harmonized dataset is focused on neurodegenerative diseases and, more specifically, on AD, PD, ALS, FTD and aging among 18,645 participants, drawn from 23 individual cohorts across a total of 31,083 unique peripheral plasma, serum and CSF samples, culminating in 35,056 unique proteomic assays and approximately 250 million individual protein measurements (Table 1 [rid=Tab1] and Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). The harmonized dataset additionally includes 40 clinical features, including demographic data, vital signs data and clinical features collected with each blood or CSF draw (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
Full Reactome enrichment summary statistics are reported in Supplementary Table 6 [this file] . 
Signature values correlated with CDR global scores (train: Pearsonʼs = 0.68; test: = 0.58) in a stepwise fashion, increasing at each level of clinical severity (Fig. 1i [rid=Fig1] ; see Supplementary Table 7 [this file] for individual-level scores). Top proteins with high feature importance in the clinical impairment signature (Fig. 1k [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ) again highlighted ACHE and NPTXR as well as additional targets linked to neuroplasticity (EPHA4 and CNTFR) and immune activation (MSMP and KLK3), underscoring their potential for transdiagnostic dementia staging. 
The clinical variables included in this first release of data include demographic data, harmonized cognitive data from research assessments and comorbidity data (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
For participants with no formal diagnosis information or CDR reported, cognitive test scores (MMSE or MoCA) were used to categorize an individual’s cognitive impairment as Not Impaired (MMSE ≥ 24 and MoCA ≥ 17) or Impaired (MMSE < 24 and MoCA < 17) (Supplementary Tables 2 [this file] and 3 [this file] ). 
After all exclusions, the final dataset comprised 5,879 Controls, 1,966 patients with AD, 607 patients with PD, 175 patients with FTD and 254 patients with ALS (Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). 
To ensure biological relevance, only aptamers targeting human proteins were retained for analysis, resulting in a final analytic set of 7,289 unique aptamers (Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
See Supplementary Table 3 [this file] for a breakdown of Controls and Patients across cohorts. 
The organ age gap was derived as the difference between predicted age and the cohort-specific locally weighted scatterplot smoothing (LOWESS) regression estimate for individuals with a normal cognitive clinical diagnosis (Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). 
CN participants did not meet criteria for any clinical diagnosis (for example, AD, MCI, FTD, ALS and PD) and had CDR = 0 and, at a minimum, cognitive test scores above a dementia threshold (MMSE ≥ 24 and/or MoCA ≥ 17) (Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ). 
Proteins associated with ε4 carriers (carrier versus non-carrier) were identified using linear regression models, adjusting for AD dementia diagnosis (CN versus AD dementia diagnosis), age, sex, contributing cohort code and mean overall protein level (Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ). The Wilcoxon rank-sum test in the ‘ggpubr’ R package (version 0.6.0) was used to test and mark the changes in protein residuals in the ε4 carrier group and the AD dementia diagnosis group (Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ) .

The MCSA is a longitudinal population-based study of cognitive aging among an age and sex stratified random sample of Olmsted County, Minnesota residents with a high retention rate ( Figure s1 [this file] ). 
A clinical diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) , dementia, or cognitively unimpaired (CU, defined as not MCI or dementia) was determined for each participant at enrollment and for all subsequent visits (see supplement [this file] ). 
In addition, to illustrate effects of combinations of predictors along with amyloid PET, we selected 5 exemplar CL values: CL 5 representing a clearly normal amyloid PET value that is common in elderly persons ( Figure s2 [this file] ); CL 25 representing a commonly used normal/abnormal threshold ; CL 50 representing the midpoint in the CL scale; CL 75; and CL 100 representing the upper benchmark value in the CL scale). 
Amyloid PET imaging was performed with Pittsburgh Compound B using previously described methods (see supplement [this file] ). 
To account for potential diagnostic misclassification at any given visit, we employed a misclassification matrix (see supplement [this file] , Table s1 [this file] ). 
See supplemental methods [this file] for further details. 
Our primary risk analysis used amyloid PET as a continuous measure but as a supplement [this file] we also summarized lifetime/absolute risk as a function of amyloid PET binarization. 
Most CU participants were APOE ε4 non-carriers and had CL values under 25 ( Figure s2 [this file] , Table s2 [this file] ). 
We recorded 1,257 transitions from CU to MCI (all in-study by definition) ( Table s3 [this file] ). 
For male CU APOE ε4 carriers at starting age 75 years, lifetime risk of MCI was 56.2% for CL 5, 60.2% for CL 25, 71.0% for CL 50, 75.2% for CL 75, and 76.5% for CL 100 and lifetime risk of dementia was 31.6% for CL 5, 35.7% for CL 25, 48.6% for CL 50, 54.5% for CL 75, and 56.5% for CL 100 ( Table s4 [this file] ). 
Similarly, 10-year absolute risk of dementia among female CU APOE ε4 carriers with CL of 50 was 2.4% for starting age 65, 19.2% for starting age 75, and 42.3% for starting age 85 ( Figure 3 [rid=F3] , Table s4 [this file] ). 
The analysis included all clinical visits for every participant, but the first amyloid PET scan was not always at the first clinical visit; these 18 participants had progressed to dementia or to a censored diagnosis at the first amyloid PET scan ( appendix [this file] pp 1–2).

To increase clarity of reporting these results, we stratified the data presentation as follows: Figure 1 [rid=F1] , 2 [rid=F2] depict only significant Odds Ratios (ORs); Supplementary Figures 6 [this file] - 11 [this file] depict all ORs and p-values; Supplementary Table 4 [this file] , 5 [this file] depict all statistical information, including ORs, p-values, and 95% confidence intervals. 
Some co-morbidities like tobacco use and congestive heart failure were robustly associated with increased depression odds for CN and dementia, but while the magnitude and direction of associations were similar for the smaller MCI subset, they were not statistically significant across 4 or more metrics ( Supplementary Figure 6 [this file] ). 
A sensitivity analysis was conducted, where any entry without all NPS metrics was removed from the analysis ( Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
For anxiety, clinical associations that were significant across at least 3 of the 4 metrics were considered ‘robust’ to metric choice ( Figure 3 [rid=F3] , 4 [rid=F4] for significant ORs; Supplementary Figure 12 [this file] - 17 [this file] for all ORs and p-values; Supplementary Tables 4 [this file] , 5 [this file] for full statistical results). 
Sleep apnea was robustly associated with higher anxiety odds for CN and dementia but not MCI, where the direction and magnitude of ORs were similarly above 1.0 but not robust ( Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ). Unlike the robust and consistent positive association with angina for depression ( Figure 3B [rid=F3] ), only CN participants had robustly increased anxiety odds with angina, though ORs for MCI and dementia were of similar magnitude and direction ( Supplementary Figure 13 [this file] ). 
Parkinson’s Disease medications were robustly associated with higher anxiety odds for MCI only, though similar, non-significant ORs were noted for CN and dementia ( Supplementary Figure 14 [this file] ). 
Sensitivity analyses had a larger effect on anxiety measures ( Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ), likely due to greatly reducing the number of available entries due to a high frequency of missing Consensus-rated metrics. 
For apathy, both the Clinician-rated and NPIQ metrics needed to be significant to suggest an association was ‘robust’ to metric choice ( Figure 5 [rid=F5] , 6 [rid=F6] for significant ORs; Supplementary Figure 18 [this file] - 23 [this file] for all ORs and p-values; Supplementary Tables 4 [this file] , 5 [this file] for full statistical results).

Apathy independent from neurodegeneration and mood disorders is rare, and so the rate of apathy was low in CN participants ( Supplementary Figure 1E [this file] , Supplementary Figure 3 [this file] ).

Some associations were no longer robust after sensitivity analyses ( Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ).

Though imperfect, to get a sense of an aggregated statistic for Jaccard+ and Jaccard− score, a Youden’s “J-like” statistic was calculated using Jaccard+ and Jaccard− scores instead of using sensitivity and specificity ( Supplementary Figure 2 [this file] ). Cohen’s Kappa was also calculated ( Supplemental Figure 3 [this file] ), though these values can be influenced by the prevalence of positive and negative ratings, as Kappa adjusts for chance agreement which itself depends on marginal distributions. 
The joint agreement across all metrics was also assessed, which is an extension of the Jaccard indices but with inclusion of 2 or more metrics ( Supplementary Figures 4 [this file] , 5 [this file] ). 
When looking at joint comparisons over two or more metrics ( Supplementary Figure 4B [this file] , D [this file] ), the three clinical gestalt metrics had higher positive agreement than almost all the combinations of the objective metrics. 
Results were similar when a Cohen’s Kappa was calculated for the GDS, where the next highest Kappa – again, >1 and =0 threshold – was about 20% lower than compared to the gold standard ( Supplementary Figure 3F [this file] ). 
Similarly for the joint comparisons ( Supplementary Figure 5B [this file] , D [this file] ), the Clinician-rated, NPIQ, and EMR/Report combination had a higher Jaccard+ than the Consensus-rated and NPIQ combination, while the combination of the Consensus-rated, Clinician-rated, and NPIQ had a higher Jaccard− compared to almost all the other pairwise combinations. 
Finally, the relative agreement of all metrics for a particular NPS was analyzed for depression ( Supplementary Figure 4B [this file] , D [this file] ) and anxiety ( Supplementary Figure 5B [this file] , D [this file] ). 
The differences in Jaccard+ and Jaccard− scores for apathy ( Supplementary Figure 4C [this file] ) mirrored those for the other NPS. 
In almost every case, the Cohen’s Kappa for the Depression, Anxiety, and Apathy metrics followed the pattern of the Jaccard+ scores ( Supplementary Figure 6 [this file] ).

The primary etiologic diagnosis in this analytical sample was AD (39%), despite lacking intermediate and advanced neuritic plaques pathology (Supplemental Table 1 [this file] ). 
Copathology or polypathology was extremely common in this sample (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] ; Supplemental Table 2 [this file] ). 
In participants with Braak B2 neurofibrillary tangles ( = 477), 25% exhibited exactly one other neuropathology ( = 115, 25.4%) and 25% exhibited two neuropathologies ( = 124, 26.1%) (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] A; Supplemental Table 2 [this file] ). A similar trend was observed in decedents with more advanced neurofibrillary tau (B3) (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] B; Supplemental Table 2 [this file] ). 
Pairwise correlations among neuropathologies were generally weak to modest (|r| < 0.3) (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] ; Supplemental Table 3 [this file] ). 
In ordinal logistic models adjusting for the same covariates, only gross infarcts were significantly associated with greater dementia severity (base model OR = 2.02, 95% CI 1.32–3.10; < 0.01), and when all five vascular lesions were entered simultaneously (fully adjusted model), the effect of gross infarcts remained (OR = 1.86, 95% CI 1.16–2.97; = 0.01) (Supplemental Table 4 [this file] ). 
In sensitivity analyses when controlling for harmonized cardiovascular disease risk, microinfarcts remained associated with lower harmonized cognition across all domains (Supplemental Table 5 [this file] ). In a sample without low neuritic plaques, microinfarcts were similarly associated with poorer memory and language scores but the effect was stronger for executive function ( =-0.48, 95% CI: -0.77 – -0.19, < 0.01) (Supplemental Table 6 [this file] ). Gross infarcts were also associated with poorer memory performance in those without low neuritic plaques ( =-0.38, 95% CI: -0.75 – -0.01, = 0.04) (Supplemental Table 6 [this file] ). The main effects of microinfarcts were similar as the primary findings when controlling for neuritic plaque levels and Braak staging (Supplemental Table 7 [this file] ). Results for microinfarcts on each cognitive domain were similar when adjusting for neuritic plaques and individual Braak stage (III (reference), IV, V, VI) (Supplemental Table 8 [this file] ) and when we added the time interval in years between the last cognitive exam and death (Supplemental Table 9 [this file] ). The effects of microinfarcts were also independent from the other four vascular neuropathologies as evidenced by the sensitivity analysis that included all vascular neuropathologies (Supplemental Table 10 [this file] ) and when controlling for the time between the last visit and death (Supplemental Table 11 [this file] ). 
None of the five vascular neuropathologies were associated with cognitive decline prior to death in those without neuritic plaques (Supplemental Table 12 [this file] ).

These variations in tremor patterns can be attributed to the fact that tremor severity is not solely determined by dopamine deficiency but is also influenced by other factors that affect its response to dopaminergic treatments . To gain a deeper understanding of different modalities in PD progression and make accurate disease progression predictions, our analyses focus on the following multiple modalities extracted from the PPMI dataset: gene data, MRI, and clinical assessment data (please refer to Supplementary 22 [this file] ).

Additionally, we obtained longitudinal sMRI scans and clinical assessments from ADNI participants (Table S2 [this file] ). For independent clinical validation, we also collected 185 MCI and 55 AD patients from the OASIS-3 dataset (Table S3 [this file] ). For more detailed information, see Figure S1 [this file] and Supplementary Method S 1 [this file] . 
All T1W images were processed using a standard voxel-based morphometry (VBM) pipeline, including anterior commissure alignment, tissue segmentation, spatial normalization, modulation, and smooth (Supplementary Method S 2 [this file] ). The Automated Anatomical Labeling (AAL) atlas was used to parcellate the cerebrum into 90 cortical and subcortical regions (Table S4 [this file] ) [ 28 [rid=CR28] ]. Next, ComBat harmonization was applied to eliminate site effects on the GMV values while preserving biological covariates of interest, including age, sex, and disease status (Supplementary Method S 3 [this file] ) [ 29 [rid=CR29] ]. 
A total of 90 regional normative models were developed to characterize age-related GMV trajectories across distinct sex groups (Supplementary Method S 4 [this file] ). 
In addition, a linear support vector machine (SVM) classifier was used to evaluate whether individual deviation patterns could differentiate diagnostic groups or predict MCI conversion (Supplementary Method S 5 [this file] ). 
Subsequently, an automatic grid search strategy was used to optimize clustering hyperparameters [ 32 [rid=CR32] , 33 [rid=CR33] ], and the product of Calinski-Harabasz Index (CHI) and Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) was used to determine the best solution (k = 2 to 10; Supplementary Method S 6 [this file] ). 
The model incorporated subject-specific and site-level random effects, and included follow-up time, subtype, and their interaction as fixed effects while controlling for age, sex, and education (Supplementary Method S 7 [this file] ). 
We further constructed subtype-related LME models to characterize longitudinal z score trajectories for each subtype and compare differences in progression patterns between subtypes (Supplementary Method S 8 [this file] ). 
As ε4 is the major genetic risk factor for AD, we used two-way ANOVA and LME model to evaluate the influence of genotype on the mean and regional z scores and their longitudinal trajectories in diagnostic groups or subtypes (Supplementary Method S 9 [this file] ). 
Gene expression data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA, http://human.brain-map.org (http://human.brain-map.org) ), including 3702 samples from six postmortem neurotypical adult brains, were processed using the pipeline [ 36 [rid=CR36] ] ( https://github.com/rmarkello/abagen (https://github.com/rmarkello/abagen) ), yielding a 90 regions × 15,633 genes expression matrix (Supplementary Method S 10 [this file] ). Statistical significance was assessed using a spatial autocorrelation-preserving spin test, and gene weights were estimated via a bootstrapping method [ 38 [rid=CR38] – 40 [rid=CR40] ] (Supplementary Method S11 [this file] ). 
To further validate the reproducibility of the main clustering results, we conducted the following strategies: (1) hierarchical clustering algorithm (Supplementary Method S 6 [this file] ); (2) other brain atlases, including AAL2 (94 cerebral regions) [ 42 [rid=CR42] ], AAL3 (140 cerebral regions) [ 43 [rid=CR43] ], Brainnetome atlas (BN246, 246 cerebral regions) [ 44 [rid=CR44] ]; (3) without ComBat harmonization; (4) validation using regional GMV extracted from sMRI data processed with the FreeSurfer pipeline (Supplementary Method S 2 [this file] ); (5) a pooled clustering analysis combining all AD and MCI participants (Supplementary Method S 12 [this file] ); (6) validation on an independent OASIS-3 dataset using the same methods as the main experiment. 
The normative models showed robust fitting performance through 10-fold cross-validation, achieving an overall standardized mean squared error of 0.63 ± 0.09 and a mean squared log-loss of -0.23 ± 0.07 (Figure S2 [this file] ). Many brain structures showed a gradual decrease in GMV during middle age, eventually progressing to widespread volumetric decline in late life (Fig. 2A [rid=Fig2] and Figure S3 [this file] ). 
The full names of the brain regions are shown in Table S4 [this file] . 
While less severe than in AD, MCI patients still showed significantly greater negative deviations in these regions than CN controls (Fig. 2C [rid=Fig2] and Figure S4 [this file] ). In the MCI group, the right amygdala had the highest negative deviation percentage (16.47%), while the CN group exhibited a lower extreme deviation percentage in any region (<4.19%) (Figure S5 [this file] ). The linear SVM based on individual deviation patterns showed good classification performance, effectively distinguishing AD from MCI and providing informative predictions for MCI conversion (Supplementary Results S 1 [this file] and Figure S6 [this file] ). 
The Gap statistic value for k = 1 was markedly lower than that for k ≥ 2 in both the AD and MCI groups, indicating the presence of non-random clustering structure (Figure S7 [this file] ). The CHI × ARI index consistently determined the optimal number of clusters is 2 for the AD (highest = 87.64) and MCI (highest = 180.42) groups (Figure S8 [this file] ). MCI-1 displayed mild positive deviations and did not differ significantly from CN controls in most regions, except the hippocampus and amygdala (Fig. 3C [rid=Fig3] and Figure S9 [this file] , P < 0.05, Bonferroni correction). From the spatial overlap maps of extreme deviations, AD-2 and MCI-2 had a significantly higher proportion of subjects with extreme negative deviations across brain regions compared to AD-1 and MCI-1 (Figure S10 [this file] ). 
Pairwise analysis revealed that MCI-2 had significantly worse performance across ten cognitive domains than MCI-1, and AD-2 was worse than AD-1 in seven domains (Fig. 4A [rid=Fig4] and Table S5 [this file] - S6 [this file] ). A higher proportion of Aβ+ &Tau+ individuals was found in AD-2 and MCI-2 compared to AD-1 and MCI-1, respectively (Fig. 4B [rid=Fig4] and Table S7 [this file] ). Additionally, MCI-2 exhibited more rapid cognitive decline than MCI-1, except for the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (RAVLT) learning scores and visuospatial ability (Fig. 4C [rid=Fig4] and Table S8 [this file] ). 
Exact P values are provided in Table S6 [this file] and S8 [this file] . 
Post hoc comparisons indicated that z scores decreased most rapidly over time in AD group, followed by MCI group, and remained stable in CN group (Fig. 5B, C [rid=Fig5] and Figure S11 [this file] ). 
Subtype analyses further identified that AD-2 and MCI-2 had significant correlations between cognitive functions and global deviation score (Supplementary Results S 2 [this file] , Figure S12 [this file] , and Table S9 [this file] - S10 [this file] ). Statistical analyses revealed significant effects of ε4 genotype on brain deviation patterns, with carriers exhibiting lower z scores and faster rates of decline than noncarriers, particularly in the MCI group and its subtypes (Supplementary Results S 3 [this file] and Figure S13 [this file] ). 
Both AD and MCI patients were consistently classified into two subtypes using different schemes, including hierarchical clustering algorithm, distinct brain atlases, and without ComBat harmonization (Figure S8 [this file] ). The ARI values were computed to assess clustering consistency, with higher values indicating better consistency (AD: 0.62-0.97; MCI: 0.60-0.97; Figure S14 [this file] ). Subtype patterns derived from regional GMV extracted using the FreeSurfer pipeline showed good agreement with those obtained from the VBM analysis (Figure S15 [this file] ). The pooled clustering analysis identified two subtypes with distinct clinical profiles and progression (Figure S16 [this file] and Table S11 [this file] ), and the subtype assignments highly aligned with those obtained within diagnostic groups (Supplementary Results S 4 [this file] and Figure S17 [this file] ). In contrast, differences between AD subtypes were less pronounced (Figure S18 [this file] ).

After observing a poor correlation between ECG and PPG-derived resting HRV (0.27), differential relationships with age, and considering evidence for higher accuracy and reliability of ECG measures compared to fingertip PPG, we decided to investigate resting HRV (via ECG) and HRV reactivity (via PPG) in separate correlational models ( Supplementary Methods 1 [this file] and Fig. 2 [rid=fcaf395-F2] ), with HRV reactivity (via PPG) most optimally represented in a latent change score model (ΔHRV) ( Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ).

There was also a positive correlation between resting HRV and the latent ‘neural’ emotion regulation factor across the whole sample that was accounted for by negative associations between these variables and age, which was driven by younger adults ( Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). 
Analogous to earlier observations, in a subsequent exploratory analysis of covariances between HRV and four previously identified latent emotionality factors in a model that incorporated all emotional reactivity and regulation task (ERRT) score variables ( Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ), only the association between resting HRV and the positive regulation latent factor was significantly different between age groups after adjustment for age ( = 8.536, df = 1, < 0.003) and was significantly negative in older adults ( = 4.8845, df = 1, = 0.0271) and positive in younger adults ( = 4.2962, df = 1, = 0.0382). Across the whole sample, age accounted for negative covariances between HRV and the positive and negative reactivity and positive regulation latent emotionality factors ( Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ).

For amyloid status in the MGB dataset, we identified six significantly associated brain regions (unadjusted < 0.05), including subcortical areas (e.g. amygdala, thalamus, ventral diencephalon), the cerebellum (cerebellar white matter and cortex) and the brainstem ( Fig. 3A [rid=fcaf210-F3] , Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). 
Meta-analyses conducted across four datasets confirmed significant associations in 14 brain areas ( Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] and Table 2 [this file] ). This analysis revealed significant overlap with dorsal attention A, control C and visual association networks ( Fig. 3F [rid=fcaf210-F3] , Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ), which are key functional systems involved in attention regulation, executive control and visual processing, respectively. 
For tau status in the presence of amyloid, we only identified two significant features, which were lateral ventricle and extracerebral CSF ( Fig. 4A [rid=fcaf210-F4] , Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). 
Next, we performed meta-analysis on brain regions with significant associations with p-tau in at least one dataset ( Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] and Table 3 [this file] ). This analysis revealed significant overlaps: increased brain volumes were associated with the somatomotor networks ( Fig. 4F [rid=fcaf210-F4] , Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ), while decreased brain volumes were associated with language and auditory networks ( Fig. 4F [rid=fcaf210-F4] , Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] ). 
Next, SCN analyses revealed no significant sex difference in any groups ( > 0.005; Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ) although network visualization exhibited stronger connections near occipital lobe in female A+T− and male A+T+ groups ( Fig. 5E [rid=fcaf210-F5] and F [rid=fcaf210-F5] ). 
Additionally, sex clustering was observed at the whole brain level in control, A+T+ and A−T−&CI in the parietal for control and A−T−&CI groups, in the temporal lobe for all groups and in the occipital lobe for A+T− and A+T+ groups ( Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ). 
In the A+T− group, females had larger volumes overlapping with the default mode network A (involved in autobiographical and prospective memory ), while males exhibited larger volumes in the frontal and parietal lobes, overlapping with the control network B (associated with executive functions and cognitive control) ( Fig. 6A–C [rid=fcaf210-F6] , Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] and Table 5 [this file] ). In the A+T+ group, females showed larger volumes in temporal and visual networks (involved in memory and visual processing), while males had overlaps with the default mode network B (linked to Theory of Mind ) ( Fig. 6D–F [rid=fcaf210-F6] , Supplementary Fig. 11 [this file] and Table 6 [this file] ). Additional analyses across the other dementia and control groups showed sex differences, with further details provided in Supplementary Fig. 12 [this file] . 
Specifically, males in the A+T− group exhibited significantly greater enlargement of the inferior lateral ventricles compared with females when contrasted with the control group ( = −0.28, = 0.005) ( Supplementary Fig. 13 [this file] ).

In ADGC data, after re-orienting ORs to be with reference to ε2/ε2 individuals (shown in Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ), a very strong increasing pattern of RRs across genotypes ε2/ε3, ε3/ε3, ε2/ε4, ε3/ε4 and ε4/ε4 was observed for risk of neuropathologically confirmed AD (Table 2 [rid=Tab2] , Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). In extended calculations that partitioned this PAF into the separate contributions of the ε3 and ε4 alleles (Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ), ε4 was estimated to account for 56.9% of neuropathologically confirmed AD burden (95% CI: 36.0%, 63.0%), with the remainder specifically attributable to ε3 (35.8%; 95% CI: 22.1%, 58.3%). Sensitivity analyses varying the assumption of baseline probability of AD from 1% to 5% among ε2 homozygotes did not markedly affect these PAF estimates (Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). 
Calculations are shown in Supplementary Tables 8 [this file] and 9 [this file] . 
This potential downward bias for ε4/ε4 individuals is reflected in the distribution of SUVr values by genotype (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ), with the mean values of ε2, ε3 and ε4 homozygotes above the Aβ+ threshold denoted.

Our goals were to understand common pathologic, clinical and genetic phenomena; therefore participants were excluded if diagnosed with any of 27 rare brain diseases ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
Four groups were defined based on Thal Aβ phase and Braak NFT stage status ( Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ): (i) AP-ADNC = Thal Aβ phase 4–5 and Braak NFT stage 0–II; (ii) typical-ADNC = Thal Aβ phase 4–5 and Braak NFT stage III–V (ADNC intermediate or high); (iii) PART-low = Thal Aβ phase 0 and Braak NFT stage 0–II; and (iv) PART-high = Thal Aβ phase 0 and Braak NFT stage III–IV. 
After exclusions were applied, 1187 participants were categorized into four groups: = 95 in group AP-ADNC; = 832 in group typical-ADNC (intermediate and high but excluding Braak stage VI); = 185 in group PART-low; and = 75 in group PART-high ( Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). Selected characteristics of each group are displayed in Supplementary Table 3 [this file] . ε4 was associated with classic ADNC, moreso than with AP-ADNC [odds ratio (OR) = 1.80 and -value = 0.004]. 
Compared with group AP-ADNC, group PART-low had lower risk of Lewy body pathology and group PART-high had lower risk of brain arteriolosclerosis ( Table 1 [rid=awae325-T1] and Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ).

The WII study is a prospective occupational cohort study of 10 308 adults, predominantly of self-reported White race (compared with Black, South Asian, and other ethnic groups), aged 35 to 55 years at baseline in 1985 to 1988. [xref] [rid=noi260027r27] An accelerometer substudy from 2012 to 2013 provided data on 4267 participants (age range, 60-83 years). [xref] [rid=noi260027r28] Details on accelerometer data, outcomes, and covariates in WII are provided in the eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
Participants were included in the analyses if they had at least 5 valid 24-hour windows (wear times during sleep and waking periods ≥2/3 of the respective periods). [xref] [rid=noi260027r31] Thirty-six metrics covering 4 SWC dimensions were derived (eTable 1 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
These included sociodemographic (age at accelerometer wear, sex, education, and marital/cohabitation status), behavioral (smoking status, alcohol consumption, and fruit and vegetable consumption), and health-related factors (body mass index, hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, central nervous system [CNS] medications, and number of chronic diseases from a list of 10 diseases) (eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
We used cubic splines to identify potential nonlinear relationships with dementia risk and included both linear and squared terms to address nonlinearity when necessary (LIPA duration, mean duration of LIPA bouts, mean duration of MVPA bouts, and sleep duration) (eFigure 1 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
A 2-step approach using Sparse Partial Least Square Deviance Residual (sPLSDR [xref] [rid=noi260027r39] ), a machine learning dimension reduction and predictor selection method for survival analysis with multicollinear data was used (eFigure 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). The second step involved selecting the optimal set of components that improved the C index of a Cox regression model including known risk factors (eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Predictive performance was evaluated using the Akaike information criterion (AIC), C index, and sensitivity for 0.75 specificity (based on Youden index categorization from model 1 to allow comparison between models) (eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
A total of 53 448 UKB participants 60 years and older (mean [SD] age, 67.5 [4.2] years; 28 989 female [54.2%]; 24 459 male [45.8%]; 323 Asian [0.6%]; 155 Black [0.3%]; 73 Chinese [0.1%]; 139 multiethnic/multiracial [0.3%]; 52 553 White [98.3%]; and 205 [0.4%] other ethnic groups), without dementia diagnosis at accelerometer measurement, and with data on covariates were included in the analyses (eFigure 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Compared with baseline UKB participants, they were somewhat healthier (eTable 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). They also had poorer values on all 4 SWC dimensions (eTable 3 and eFigure 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Nine of the 36 metrics contributed to 2 components reflecting the most informative, nonredundant SWC features with a sparsity of 0.85 (eFigure 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] ) and improved dementia prediction in UKB data. The factor weights of 9 metrics in SWC components are shown in Figure 1 [rid=noi260027f1] and eTable 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
Exclusion of dementia cases in the first 2 years of follow-up led to similar results (eTable 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
The SWC components were associated with higher dementia risk across most subgroups (eFigure 6 in Supplement 1 [this file] ), and adding them to model 1 significantly improved the C index in all subgroups except the group with low education, with gains ranging from 0.011 to 0.029 ( Figure 2 [rid=noi260027f2] ). 
In WII, among 3965 participants (mean [SD] age, 69.4 [5.7] years; 1025 female [25.9%]; 2940 male [74.1%]; 97 Black [2.4%]; 160 South Asian [4.0%]; 3671 White [92.7%]; and 32 other ethnic groups [0.8%]) in the analyses (eFigure 7 in Supplement 1 [this file] ), 346 (8.7%) developed dementia over a mean (SD) follow-up of 10.6 (2.4) years ( Table 1 [rid=noi260027t1] ). Removing dementia cases in the first 2 years of follow-up yielded similar results (eTable 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Both SWC components were associated with higher dementia risk across most subgroups (eFigure 8 in Supplement 1 [this file] ), and adding them to model 1 improved predictive performance in all subgroups, although the change was not always statistically significant (ie, in younger participants, those with intermediate/high education, and with depressive symptoms) ( Figure 3 [rid=noi260027f3] ). 
Adding SWC components to an age-only model improved the predictive value in UKB (ΔC index = 0.026; 95% CI, 0.016-0.035) and in WII (ΔC index = 0.023; 95% CI, 0.011-0.034); this increase was higher than that for sex or education (ΔC indexes = 0.000 to 0.002 in both cohorts) and similar to that for in UKB (ΔC index = 0.033; 95% CI, 0.022-0.044) and in WII (ΔC index = 0.024; 95% CI, 0.012-0.036), MMSE in WII (ΔC index = 0.020; 95% CI, 0.011-0.029), and p-tau217 in WII (ΔC index = 0.039; 95% CI, 0.020-0.058), with no significant differences in ΔC index between these prediction models (eTable 6 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Only component 1 improved the C index for mortality in both cohort studies and incident CVD in UKB (eTable 7 in Supplement 1 [this file] ).

We examined associations between psychological distress, cognition and dementia using a multi-cohort approach, and included data from five longitudinal studies ( Table S2 [this file] ): the Caerphilly Prospective Study (CAPS), the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA), Whitehall II (WHII), the National Child Development Study (NCDS); and the National Survey of Health and Development (NSHD). 
Self-reported psychological distress at baseline was measured using validated assessment tools within each study, as reported in Table S3 [this file] and Supplementary Information [this file] . 
To allow comparison across waves, in line with guidance from CLS and CLOSER, we created harmonised variables based on seven conceptually similar items capturing psychological distress consistently within each measure, with items pertaining to low mood, fatigue, tense/stressed, sleep problems, panic, hopelessness and health anxiety ( Supplementary Information [this file] ). 
We also examined associations with clinically-significant psychological distress using binary variables based on validated cut-off scores on questionnaires within each study ( Table S3 [this file] ; Supplementary Information [this file] ). 
Full information about assessments of individual cognitive domains within each study is provided in Supplementary Information [this file] . 
Further detail about dementia ascertainment is provided in Supplementary Information [this file] . 
Full information about covariates within each study is provided in Supplementary Information [this file] . 
Before analysis, we harmonised all variables between studies as far as possible ( Supplementary Information [this file] ). We applied multiple imputation models using chained equations to impute missing covariate data ( Table S4 [this file] ). 
A participant flow diagram is provided in Figure S1 [this file] , indicating participants excluded due to having dementia at baseline, missing information on baseline psychological distress, or without information on either cognition in the single time point used in analyses or at least two cognitive assessments after baseline psychological distress assessment. For instance, those excluded were more likely to have lower education, manual occupations, comorbidities, and to have negative health behaviours ( Table S5 [this file] ). 
First, we investigated associations between baseline psychological distress and general fluid cognitive level at a single time point (mean ages 62–72 years; Table 2 [rid=T2] ; Figure 1 [rid=F1] ; Figures S2 [this file] – S3 [this file] ). 
Second, we examined associations between psychological distress and subsequent general fluid cognitive change in ELSA, NSHD and WHII ( Table 2 [rid=T2] ; Figure S4 [this file] ). 
Third, we examined associations between psychological distress and subsequent dementia in CAPS, ELSA, WHII and NSHD ( Table 2 [rid=T2] ; Figures 2 [rid=F2] – 3 [rid=F3] ; Figure S5 [this file] – S7 [this file] ). 
Patterns of association were similar when examining depression and anxiety symptoms individually ( Figure S3 [this file] , Figure S7 [this file] ).

Participants for MRI-Wave-2 were included in the analyses if they participated in the 2019 wave of the Whitehall II Study, had good-quality scans without significant incidental findings at MRI-Wave-1, had no MRI contraindications, no contraindications to the hypercapnia challenge, and no diagnosis of dementia (Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S1). 
Aortic scans (Additional file 1 [this file] : Method S1) of the proximal ascending aorta used a 4-MHz cardiac transducer on a GE VIVID 7 system (November 2019–January 2023, = 112). Carotid scans (Additional file 1 [this file] : Method S2) used a 13-MHz linear transducer on a GE VIVID 7 system (November 2019–January 2023, = 112) and Zonare Z.One System (January 2023–May 2023, = 51). Aortic and left and right carotid measures included arterial diameter (mm), pulse wave velocity (m/s), arterial compliance (mm /kPA), distensibility (10 kPa), and beta stiffness index (equations in Additional file 1 [this file] : Method S3). Summary measures were derived using principal component analysis (PCA, see details in Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S2). 
For details of the brain measures, see Additional file 1 [this file] : Method S4. 
Details of the tests are presented in the protocol papers for MRI-Wave-1 [ 32 [rid=CR32] ] and MRI-Wave-2 [ 28 [rid=CR28] ], as well as in Additional file 1 [this file] : Method S5. We performed a principal component analysis (PCA) to combine large quantities of data from the cognitive tests and subscales into meaningful cognitive domains and reduce the dimensionality (detailed derivations are described below and in Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S2). 
Based on factor loadings, scree plots, eigenvalues, and cumulative explained variance, we derived three factors each for the carotid and aorta: stiffness (comprising beta stiffness index and pulse wave velocity), diameter (systolic and diastolic diameter), compliance (comprising distensibility and compliance) (Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S2). 
We derived six cognitive factors: episodic memory, working memory, executive function, visuospatial memory, verbal fluency, and lexical retrieval (Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S2). 
Among the 163 participants, 42 (25.8%) were women, and the mean (SD) age was 68.2 (4.4) years at MRI-Wave-1 and 76.9 (4.5) years at MRI-Wave-2 (Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S1 and demographics in Table 1 [rid=Tab1] ). Aorta scans were available for 89 participants due to change in equipment during the study, and carotid scans for 153 participants (Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S1 and demographics in Table 1 [rid=Tab1] ). For a summary of demographic variables across the low FRS and moderate-high FRS risk groups, see Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S1.

The 3T MRI scans were obtained shortly after wave 11 for 775 participants according to the published protocol (eMethods 1 and eTable 1 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
The sample selection flowchart is provided in eMethods 2 and eFigure 1 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
Scoring criteria for the AHEI-2010 and its distribution are described in eMethods 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
We used linear mixed-effects models with maximum likelihood estimation to extract the intercept (projected diet at wave 3) and slope (change in diet over time from middle to older age) for diet and WHR; individual trajectories are shown in eFigure 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] . The best-fit model was the linear model for diet and a natural cubic spline model with 2 for WHR (eMethods 4, eTables 2-4, and eFigure 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
We extracted global FA, radial diffusivity (RD), axial diffusivity (AD), and mean diffusivity (MD) from the mean tract-based spatial statistics skeleton as proxy markers of myelin integrity (eMethods 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Hippocampal functional connectivity was analyzed using seed-based correlation analyses with a hippocampus seed mask, which was smoothed using a kernel sphere of 4 mm radius (eMethods 5 and eFigure 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] ) with 1000 permutations. 
In that case, we tested those brain connectivity mediators (M) that were associated with AHEI-2010 or WHR (X→M) (eMethods 6 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
AHEI-2010 analyses were adjusted for total energy intake (kcal/d) (eMethods 7 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
The WHR cohort included 532 males (80.1%) and 132 females (19.9%), with a mean (SD) age of 47.7 (5.1) years at wave 3, 67.9 (5.1) years at wave 11, and 69.8 (5.1) years at MRI scan (eTable 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
The mean outcome measures (white matter metrics, cognitive performance, and hippocampus connectivity maps) are shown in eTable 6 and eFigure 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
Better midlife diet was, however, associated with higher functional connectivity between the left hippocampus and occipital lobe and cerebellum (clusters 1-7; 8-2648 mm ; total: 9176 mm ; < .05) and 1 small cluster between the right hippocampus and cerebellum (cluster 1; 136 mm ; = .04) ( Figure 2 [rid=zoi250018f2] ; eTable 9 and eFigure 7 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Higher AHEI-2010 slopes (ie, individual improvements in diet quality across 11 years) were associated with higher FA (clusters 1-6; 32-8760 mm ; total: 19 432 mm ; < .05), lower MD (clusters 1-10; 48-2456 mm ; total: 5560 mm ; < .05), and lower AD (clusters 1-2; 32-2568 mm ; total: 2600 mm ; < .045) in several white matter tracts ( Figure 3 [rid=zoi250018f3] ; eFigure 6 and eTable 7 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Associations with MD were observed in the optic radiation and the superior parietal lobe (eTable 7 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). ROI analyses of the 3 predefined hippocampal tracts showed that AD in fornix was associated with AHEI-2010 slopes (β [SE] = 0.26 [0.11]; FDR-corrected = .02 (eTable 8 in Supplement 1 [this file] ; Figure 4 [rid=zoi250018f4] A). Improvement in diet (higher slope) was associated with better lexical fluency before FDR adjustment (β [SE] = 0.01 [0.00]; FDR-corrected = .21) (eTable 10 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
However, higher mean AHEI-2010 scores were associated with higher left hippocampal functional connectivity to clusters in the occipital lobe and right cerebellum (clusters 1-10; 8-1104 mm ; total: 2472 mm ; < .05) (eFigures 7 and 8 and eTable 9 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Higher WHR in midlife (ie, higher intercept) was associated with higher MD and RD covering 26.4% (333 088 mm , < .001) and 23.1% (291 888 mm , < .05; clusters 1-15, 48-278 688 mm , total: 291 888 mm , < .05) of the total white matter tracts, respectively, and with lower FA covering 4.9% (clusters 1-23; 8-25 544 mm ; total: 61 272 mm ; < .05) of the white matter skeleton ( Figure 5 [rid=zoi250018f5] ; eFigure 6 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). The maxima for the direct associations with MD and RD were identified in the cingulum and SLF and ILF (eTable 7 in Supplement 1 [this file] ), whereas the maxima for inverse associations with FA were in the corticospinal tract. We also noted 1 small cluster (0.03% of white matter tract, <50 voxels) showing an inverse association with MD in the corticospinal tract (eFigure 6 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). ROI analyses revealed that higher WHR intercepts were also associated with lower FA and higher RD in the ILF (FA: β [SE] = –14.52 [4.82]; 95% CI, –23.98 to –5.06; FDR-corrected = .003]; RD: β [SE] = 9.11 [3.33]; 95% CI, 2.57-15.65; FDR-corrected = .006]) and with lower FA and higher MD and RD in the cingulum (FA: β [SE] = –3.08 [1.21]; 95% CI, –5.44 to –0.71; FDR-corrected = .011]; MD: β [SE] = 4.28 [1.34]; 95% CI, 1.64-6.92; FDR-corrected = .002]; RD: β [SE] = 3.66 [1.15]; 95% CI, 1.40-5.91; FDR-corrected = .002]) (eTable 8 in Supplement 1 [this file] ; Figure 4 [rid=zoi250018f4] A). However, higher intercepts (higher midlife WHR) were associated with lower cognitive performance on the verbal episodic memory (β [SE] = –0.02 [0.01]; 95% CI, –0.03 to –0.01; FDR-corrected = .003), digit span (β [SE] = –0.02 [0.01]; 95% CI, –0.03 to –0.01; FDR-corrected = .002), semantic fluency (β [SE] = –0.02 [0.01]; 95% CI, –0.03 to –0.01; FDR-corrected = .007), digit coding (β [SE] = –0.01 [0.00]; 95% CI, –0.01 to 0.00; FDR-corrected = .001), and trail making (β [SE] = 0.15 [0.07]; 95% CI, 0.01-0.29; FDR-corrected = .04) tests ( Figure 4 [rid=zoi250018f4] B; eTable 10 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
WHR slope was associated with digit span (β [SE] = 0.02 [0.01]; 95% CI, 0.00-0.03; = .03), but this association did not survive FDR adjustment (FDR-corrected = .16) (eTable 10 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
We examined whether the observed FDR-corrected associations between WHR intercept and cognition (eTable 10 in Supplement 1 [this file] ) were mediated by the MRI variables associated with WHR intercepts (eTables 7 and 8 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). For detailed sample selection and inclusion/exclusion criteria, please see online supplemental figure 1 [this file] and the online supplemental methods [this file] . 
UKB field IDs used for diagnosis and the list of International Classification of Disease ninth revision (ICD-9) and ICD 10th revision (ICD-10) codes are presented in the online supplemental table 1 [this file] . In the WHII sample, dementia diagnosis was determined through self-report and hospital inpatient records [xref] [rid=R16] ( online supplemental methods [this file] , and online supplemental table 1 [this file] ). 
The full list of predictors’ detailed descriptions including UKB field codes are in online supplemental methods [this file] and online supplemental table 2 [this file] . 
The predictive ability of the UKBDRS was compared with that of three existing risk scores: the DRS, [xref] [rid=R9] ANU-ADRI, [xref] [rid=R10] and CAIDE. [xref] [rid=R11] We computed the three risk scores in the UKB and WHII cohorts using the formulae reported in the respective original papers ( online supplemental methods [this file] ). 
The first stage (‘variable selection’) used only the training set and involved submitting the 28 candidate predictors to a least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) Cox regression ( online supplemental methods [this file] ), to identify a parsimonious model with dementia as the outcome. [xref] [rid=R18] Correlation between numerical variables was assessed before LASSO ( online supplemental methods [this file] , online supplemental figure 2 [this file] ). LASSO selected variables were then used as predictors in a Fine and Gray competing risk regression model. [xref] [rid=R19] Duration of follow-up was calculated as time between baseline and either date of dementia, death, or censoring date ( online supplemental methods [this file] ). The linear predictor was used to compute the predicted probability of developing dementia ( online supplemental methods [this file] ). Assumptions were checked as described in online supplemental methods [this file] ( online supplemental figures 3 and 4 [this file] ). 
Based on available follow-up times, we evaluated AUC at a 14-year time horizon in UKB and 17-year in WHII ( online supplemental methods [this file] ). 
We used risk calibration to assess the agreement between the observed proportion of dementia cases and predicted probabilities of developing dementia as calculated from the risk score [xref] [rid=R21] ( online supplemental methods [this file] ). 
The sample characteristics are in online supplemental table 3 [this file] , and participant selection is in online supplemental figure 1 [this file] ; 3813 (1.7%) and 93 (3.2%) participants developed dementia in the UKB and WHII cohorts, respectively. There were significant differences in age, sex, and education between included and excluded participants in UKB and WHII ( online supplemental table 4 [this file] ). 
LASSO regression identified 11 variables as predictive of incident dementia: age, education, history of diabetes, history/current depression, history of stroke, parental history of dementia, Townsend deprivation, hypertension, high cholesterol, household occupancy (living alone), and sex ( online supplemental table 5 [this file] ). 
Sensitivity analyses showed that the UKBDRS performed better in predicting dementia within 14 years compared with prediction of dementia within shorter time horizons of 5 years (AUC 0.75, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.78) or 10 years (AUC 0.76, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.78) ( online supplemental table 6 [this file] ). 
In sensitivity analyses conducted in the WHII sample, the UKBDRS model outperformed CAIDE but performed similarly to the DRS and ANU-ADRI in individuals over 60 ( online supplemental table 7 [this file] ). Online supplemental table 8 [this file] presents sensitivity, specificity, negative predictive value (NPV) and positive predictive value (PPV) of both UKBDRS scores at various thresholds. UKBDRS models were well-calibrated—that is, they had an intercept and slope close to 0 and 1, respectively ( online supplemental table 9 and figure 5 [this file] ). 
Individuals can also be classified into low-risk and high-risk groups, according to sensitivity and specificity thresholds reported in online supplemental table 9 [this file] .

Baseline assessments included all components of the CAIDE, BDSI, and ANU-ADRI scores, measured according to standard operating protocols, as detailed in the eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] . Dementia was ascertained using primary and secondary diagnoses from linked hospital admission data and from underlying and contributory causes of death being dementia (eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
We determined 4 dementia risk scores (CAIDE clinical version, CAIDE– -supplemented version, BDSI, and ANU-ADRI) for each participant using standard formulas and analyzed each risk score separately, excluding participants with missing data on any of the items in the risk score under investigation (eTable 1 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
For each risk score, we calculated detection rate, false-positive rate, the number of participants with incident dementia but with a negative test result per 10 participants with incident dementia, and the ratio of true to false positives (eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Syntax for the analyses is provided in the eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] . values were 2-sided, and statistical significance was set at = .05. 
The associations between risk score quintiles and dementia incidence followed a dose-response pattern, but the gradient was steeper using only information from participant’s age (eTable 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Incident dementia numbers are presented in eTable 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
In subgroups of middle-aged (aged ≤64 years at baseline) and older (aged ≥65 years at baseline) participants, the performance of the risk scores was similar or worse than in the total sample (eTable 4 and eTable 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). The findings did not change after including incident dementia from the first year of follow-up (eTable 6 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
C statistics ranged from 0.52 (95% CI, 0.50-0.54) to 0.60 (95% CI, 0.58-0.62) (eTable 7 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Estimates for 20-year dementia prediction in this younger cohort of 4865 participants were not materially different from those in the main analysis, except that the true to false positives ratio improved owing to a greater proportion of participants with incident dementia in this cohort (eTable 8 in Supplement 1 [this file] ).
